title: Your First Program, and Every Word in It
lead:
You will write this exam by hand, with no compiler to correct you. So the
skeleton has to come out of your pen without thinking, the way your signature does. That is
all this lesson is: eight words you will write on every answer for the rest of the week.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write a complete, correct Java program on blank paper: the class wrapper, the main line spelled exactly right, a statement that prints something, and every brace and semicolon in place.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a
frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to check. One step at a time.

frames.teach:
Java runs nothing on its own. Every instruction must live inside a method, and every method must live inside a class. So the smallest possible program is already three layers deep. Here is the whole shape, and nothing else is ever added to it.

public class NameOfFile {          <- must match the file name    public static void main(String[] args) {        // your statements go here, one per line, each ending in ;    }}
frames.ask: Which of those three lines actually does something?

frames.teach:
They are the container. The work goes on the line marked with the comment, inside both sets of braces. Now the real thing.

public class Hello {    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("Hello, world");    }}
OutputHello, world
frames.ask: Count the braces. How many open, and how many close?

frames.teach: One pair for the class, one pair for main, and they nest: the inner pair closes before the outer one. Every brace you open must be closed, and in the hall nothing will remind you.
frames.ask:
So when you write the opening brace of a class, what should you write
immediately?

frames.teach: on its own line, before you write anything inside. Then you fill the middle. That one habit removes the commonest compile error there is. Now the line that carries the marks: public static void main(String[] args).
frames.ask: Say what you think each of those five words is doing, then read on.

frames.check: Here they are, and you must learn them.
frames.teach:
WordWhat it means
publicanything may call this, including the machinery that starts your program
staticit belongs to the class itself, so it can run without an object being made first
voidit hands nothing back when it finishes
mainthe name Java looks for. Spelt any other way, the program compiles and refuses to start
String[] argsa row of text values handed in from the command line. You will never use it, and you must never leave it out
frames.ask: If you wrote Main instead of main, would it compile?

frames.check: Yes, and it would still not run.
frames.teach: That is the nastiest kind of error: nothing is wrong with the code, there is simply no starting point. Java is case sensitive everywhere: main, Main and MAIN are three different names, and so are score and Score.

Now the statement itself. System.out.println("Hello, world"); reads right to left: print this line, of the output, of the System. Notice the semicolon. Every statement ends in one, and a missing semicolon is the single most common error in a handwritten exam script.
frames.ask: Does the line public class Hello { need a semicolon?

frames.teach:
A line that ends in an opening brace is not
a statement, it is a heading for a block. Semicolons go on statements only: assignments,
calls, returns.
frames.ask: There are two printing calls. What is the difference between println and print?

frames.check: println moves to a new line afterwards, print does not.
frames.teach:
public class Three {    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("one");        System.out.println("two");        System.out.print("three");        System.out.print(" and four");    }}
Outputone
two
three and four

Look at the last line of output: three and and four ran together, because print left the cursor where it was.
frames.ask:
Which one would you use to print a label and then read an answer on the
same line?

frames.teach: so the prompt and the typing sit together. Two last things. A comment is a note to the reader that the compiler ignores: // to the end of the line, or /* ... */ across several.
frames.ask: Why does this matter in an exam rather than at a keyboard?

frames.check: Because the paper asks for them.
frames.teach:
The instruction
on the last paper says to use comments in Sections B and C to say what each block of code
does. That is free marks for a habit that costs you five seconds a block.
frames.ask: Last one. What must the file be called if the class is Hello?

frames.teach:
A public class
must live in a file of its own name. You are writing on paper, so no file exists, but the
examiner still expects the class name and the stated file name to agree.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The skeleton, from memory, every time
blocks.html:
Write this out ten times tonight. Not read: written. It is the opening of every program you will produce this week and in the hall.

public class Hello {    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("Hello, world");    }}

The order you should write it in: the class line and its closing brace, then the main line and its closing brace, then the statements in the middle. Braces first, contents second, and you will never lose one.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: The four that cost marks every year
blocks.html:
• A missing semicolon. Every statement, every time.
  • An unclosed brace. Write the pair before you write the contents.
  • Main, Println, string. Case is part of the name. String is capital S; println is all lower case.
  • Leaving out String[] args. It looks unused, and the program will not start without it.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Write, on paper, a complete program called Greet that prints your name. Then check every brace and every semicolon.

2. What are the five words of the main line, in order, and what does each mean?

3. Which of these needs a semicolon: public class X {, int a = 5, }?

4. What is printed by two print calls, one after the other?
blocks.answer: 1. public class Greet { then public static void main(String[] args) { then the println, then two closing braces. 2. public, static, void, main, String[] args; see the table above. 3. Only int a = 5, which needs one at the end. 4. Both on the same line, with nothing between them.

blocks.big:
Class, then main, then statements. Braces in pairs, semicolons on statements,
and every letter in the right case.
blocks.sub: Write the skeleton from memory before you read tomorrow's lesson. If it does not come out clean, write it again.

title: What Java Is, and the JDK, JRE and JVM
lead:
Pure recall, and cheap. The objective section asks about this every year, and
it costs you fifteen minutes to own for good. Then you will not meet it again.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Say what Java is in one sentence, explain what the JDK, the JRE and the JVM each are and how they nest, and describe the journey from your source file to a running program, naming bytecode and the two tools that make it.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: You type a file called Hello.java. It is plain text, and a processor cannot run plain text. So something must translate it.
frames.ask: Name the tool that does that translation.

frames.teach: But here is what makes Java different from most languages: it does not translate your file into instructions for your processor. It translates it into bytecode, a set of instructions for an imaginary machine, and saves it as Hello.class.
frames.ask:
If bytecode is for an imaginary machine, what has to exist for it to
run?

frames.check: A program that pretends to be that machine.
frames.teach: That is the Java Virtual Machine, the JVM, and it is what the command java starts. It reads the bytecode and carries it out on your real processor.
frames.ask:
Why is that worth doing, instead of compiling straight to machine
code?

frames.check: Because the bytecode then runs anywhere.
frames.teach: Any machine with a JVM can run the same .class file, whatever processor or operating system it has. That is the promise Java is famous for: write once, run anywhere, and it is the answer to "what makes Java platform independent".
frames.ask: So which part is the platform dependent one?

frames.teach: There is a different JVM for Windows, for Linux, for a phone; your bytecode does not change. Now the three initials, which the paper asks you to distinguish. They nest, and drawing that is the whole answer.
frames.ask:
Which do you need to WRITE a program, and which to merely RUN
one?

frames.check: The JDK to write, the JRE to run.
frames.teach: That is the sentence to give in the exam. Now the journey, end to end.
frames.ask: At which arrow would a spelling mistake in your code be caught?

frames.teach: Java is compiled, so the whole file is checked before anything runs at all. A syntax error means nothing runs, not even the correct lines above it. That is the opposite of an interpreted language, and it is a favourite comparison question.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The five sentences that answer this whole topic
blocks.html:
• Java is a high level, object oriented, platform independent programming language that is compiled to bytecode and executed by a virtual machine.
  • The JDK is the Java Development Kit: the JRE plus the development tools, principally the compiler javac. You need it to write programs.
  • The JRE is the Java Runtime Environment: the JVM plus the standard class libraries. You need it to run programs.
  • The JVM is the Java Virtual Machine: the program that actually executes bytecode, and the only part that differs from platform to platform.
  • Write once, run anywhere: javac turns source into bytecode, and any JVM on any machine can run that same bytecode.

Other features worth naming if asked: it is simple (no pointers, no manual memory freeing), secure (code runs inside the JVM's sandbox), robust (strong type checking and exception handling), multithreaded, and it has automatic garbage collection, so memory you stop using is reclaimed for you.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: It does not. javac compiles; the JVM executes. Getting those two the wrong way round is the commonest way to lose an otherwise free mark. And the JVM does not read your .java file at all: it never sees your source, only the .class bytecode.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. What does javac produce, and what runs it?

2. Put JDK, JRE and JVM in order, largest first, and say what each adds.

3. What exactly makes Java platform independent?

4. Your program has a spelling mistake on line 40. How much of it runs?
blocks.answer: 1. Bytecode, in a .class file; the JVM runs it. 2. JDK contains JRE contains JVM; the JVM executes bytecode, the JRE adds the class libraries, the JDK adds the compiler and tools. 3. The bytecode is the same everywhere, and a platform specific JVM executes it. 4. None of it. Java is compiled, so the error is found before execution starts.

blocks.big:
javac compiles to bytecode, the JVM runs bytecode. JDK holds JRE holds JVM.
Write once, run anywhere.
blocks.sub: Draw the three nested boxes and the four-word journey from memory. That drawing is the answer to every question on this topic.

blocks.label: Now prove it
blocks.tag: every objective question on this topic

title: Variables, and the Eight Types
lead:
In Java, unlike Python, you must say what kind of thing every box holds
before you put anything in it. That is one extra word per line, and it is where half the
find-the-errors marks live: the examiner plants a value that does not fit its box.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Declare a variable of any type and name it legally; list the eight primitive types with their sizes; say which type any expression produces; convert between types and know which direction needs a cast; and use final for a constant.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A variable is a named box that holds one value. You make one by writing the type, then the name, then optionally = and a value: int score = 72;. The type is a promise about what may ever go in that box, and Java holds you to it.
frames.ask:
What three parts does that line have, in
order?

frames.teach:
Here are the five you will actually use, all at once.

public class Types {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int count = 20;        double price = 19.99;        char grade = 'A';        boolean passed = true;        String name = "Ada";        System.out.println(count);        System.out.println(price);        System.out.println(grade);        System.out.println(passed);        System.out.println(name);    }}
Output20
19.99
A
true
Ada

Note the quotes: double quotes for a String, single for a char, and a char holds exactly one character.
frames.ask: What would char grade = "A"; do?

frames.teach: "A" is a String, and a String does not fit in a char box. That is exactly the planted error to look for. Now the full set. Java has eight primitive types, and the paper asks for them with their sizes.
frames.ask: Before you look: how many bytes do you think an int takes?

frames.teach:
and here is the whole family, measured by the JVM itself rather than quoted from a table.

public class Sizes {    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("byte  " + Byte.SIZE / 8 + " bytes");        System.out.println("short " + Short.SIZE / 8 + " bytes");        System.out.println("int   " + Integer.SIZE / 8 + " bytes");        System.out.println("long  " + Long.SIZE / 8 + " bytes");        System.out.println("float " + Float.SIZE / 8 + " bytes");        System.out.println("double " + Double.SIZE / 8 + " bytes");        System.out.println("int max is " + Integer.MAX_VALUE);    }}
Outputbyte  1 bytes
short 2 bytes
int   4 bytes
long  8 bytes
float 4 bytes
double 8 bytes
int max is 2147483647
frames.ask:
There is one primitive missing from that output. Which, and
why?

frames.teach: whose size the language deliberately does not define; it holds only true or false. The eighth is char, two bytes, because Java characters are Unicode.
frames.ask: Is String one of the eight?

frames.check: No, and this is worth a mark.
frames.teach: String is a class, not a primitive: hence its capital letter, while every primitive is lower case. A primitive holds a value directly; a String variable holds a reference to an object. Keep that distinction, because Lesson 2.9 turns on it.

Now moving a value from one type of box to another. Going from a smaller box to a bigger one is always safe, so Java does it silently: that is widening. Going the other way can lose information, so Java refuses unless you insist with a cast, (int). 

public class Narrowing {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int whole = 7;        double real = whole;          // widening: always safe        System.out.println(real);        double money = 19.99;        int pounds = (int) money;     // narrowing: needs a cast, and CHOPS        System.out.println(pounds);    }}
frames.ask:
Predict both lines of output
below.

frames.teach:
Output7.0
19

Look hard at the second one: (int) 19.99 is 19, not 20. A cast to int chops the decimal part off; it does not round.
frames.ask:
How would you round 19.99 to the nearest whole number
instead?

frames.teach:
which gives 20.
Chopping when you meant rounding is a silent error: nothing crashes, the number is simply
wrong.
frames.ask: Now naming. Which of these are legal variable names: total, 2ndScore, my score, _count, class?

frames.teach: The rules: a name may contain letters, digits, _ and $; it may not start with a digit; it may not contain a space; and it may not be a Java keyword, which is why class is out.
frames.ask:
By convention, how is a variable name written when it has two words in
it?

frames.teach:
lower case first letter, capital for each word after. Classes get a capital first letter, BankAccount. Constants are shouted. Which brings us to the last idea.

public class Consts {    public static void main(String[] args) {        final double VAT = 0.075;        double price = 200;        System.out.println(price * (1 + VAT));    }}
Output215.0

final means the value can never be changed after it is set: assigning to it again will not compile.
frames.ask: What is the naming convention for a final?

frames.teach: with underscores between words: MAX_SIZE, VAT. Use one wherever a number in your program has a meaning, and the examiner will see that you meant it.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
TypeSizeHoldsExample
byte1 bytewhole numbers, −128 to 127byte b = 100;
short2 byteswhole numbersshort s = 5000;
int4 byteswhole numbers, the default choiceint n = 72;
long8 bytesvery large whole numberslong L = 90000L;
float4 bytesdecimals, less precisefloat f = 1.5f;
double8 bytesdecimals, the default choicedouble d = 19.99;
char2 bytesone character, single quoteschar c = 'A';
booleannot definedtrue or falseboolean ok = true;

Two suffixes you must not forget: a long literal ends in L and a float literal ends in f. Without them, float f = 1.5; will not compile, because 1.5 is a double.

Widening is free, narrowing needs a cast: byte to short to int to long to float to double is automatic; going back the other way needs (int) and chops.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
An array or a variable declared int and then filled with values that have decimal points:

int[] arr = {24.0, 40.0, 66.0};   // will not compile

That is on the 2025/2026 paper, word for word, in Question One. The fix is either double[] or values without the decimal points, and the fix you choose has to match the rest of the program: if a total is later declared int, changing the array to double breaks that line too. Say so in your answer; it is the difference between spotting one error and understanding the segment.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. List the eight primitives with their sizes.

2. What is (int) 9.99?

3. Why will float f = 1.5; not compile, and what fixes it?

4. Which are legal names: 1stPrize, prize1, final, total_score?
blocks.answer: 1. byte 1, short 2, int 4, long 8, float 4, double 8, char 2, boolean undefined. 2. 9; a cast chops. 3. 1.5 is a double, which does not fit a float without help; write 1.5f. 4. prize1 and total_score; the first starts with a digit and final is a keyword.

blocks.big:
Type, name, value. Eight primitives, capital String is not one of them.
Widening is free, narrowing needs a cast and chops.
blocks.sub: When you sweep a broken listing, check every value against the box it is going into. That one habit finds most of the planted errors.

title: Operators, and the Integer Division Trap
lead:
Four of these surprise people, and all four are planted in exam listings
every year. Learn the four surprises and the dry-run questions stop being guesses.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Evaluate any arithmetic, relational or logical expression by hand and say what type the answer is; know exactly what integer division does; tell a++ from ++a; and know when + adds and when it joins.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: The five arithmetic operators are + - * / %. Four behave.
frames.ask: What do you expect 7 / 2 to be in Java?

frames.teach:
This is the first and worst surprise. When both sides are integers, Java does integer division and throws the remainder away. The remainder is what % gives you.

public class IntDiv {    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println(7 / 2);        System.out.println(7 % 2);        System.out.println(7.0 / 2);        System.out.println((double) 7 / 2);        int total = 7, n = 2;        System.out.println((double) total / n);    }}
Output3
1
3.5
3.5
3.5
frames.ask: Lines 3, 4 and 5 all give 3.5. What made the difference?

frames.teach: If either operand is a double, the whole division is done in doubles. So you fix integer division either by making a literal a double (7.0) or by casting one side, (double) total / n.
frames.ask: Where does the cast have to go in (double) total / n, and why not (double) (total / n)?

frames.check: On one operand, before the division happens.
frames.teach:
(double)(total / n) divides first, in integers, loses the remainder, and then converts the already-wrong answer. Here is the whole mistake in one program.

public class Average {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int sum = 250;        int count = 4;        System.out.println("wrong: " + sum / count);        System.out.println("right: " + (double) sum / count);    }}
Outputwrong: 62
right: 62.5

An average of 62 instead of 62.5. Nothing crashed.
frames.ask: Which of these would you write for an average of two ints?

frames.teach:
Second surprise: + means two different things.

public class PlusTwo {    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println(1 + 2 + " marks");        System.out.println("marks: " + 1 + 2);    }}
Output3 marks
marks: 12
frames.ask: Why did the first give 3 marks and the second give marks: 12?

frames.teach: In the first, 1 + 2 are both numbers so they add, and the result is then joined to the text. In the second, the leftmost + already has text on one side, so it joins, and then joins again. If either side is a String, + joins. Wrap arithmetic in brackets whenever it sits next to text: "total: " + (1 + 2).
Third surprise: ++ and -- come in two flavours. a++ is post increment: use the old value, then add one. ++a is pre increment: add one, then use the new value.
frames.ask: If a is 5, what does System.out.println(a++) print, and what is a afterwards?

frames.teach:
public class Incr {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int a = 5;        System.out.println(a++);        System.out.println(a);        int b = 5;        System.out.println(++b);        System.out.println(b);    }}
Output5
6
6
6

On its own line as a statement, a++; and ++a; do exactly the same thing. The difference only shows when the value is used in the same expression, which is precisely where an exam puts it.
frames.ask: So in i++ at the end of a for loop, does it matter which you write?

frames.teach: Nothing uses the value there. Now the relational operators, == != > < >= <=, every one of which produces a boolean.
frames.ask: What is the difference between = and ==?

frames.teach:
Writing if (x = 5) in Java will not compile, because an assignment gives an int and if demands a boolean, which is a small mercy. Now the logical operators.

public class Logic {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int age = 20;        boolean member = false;        System.out.println(age >= 18 && member);        System.out.println(age >= 18 || member);        System.out.println(!member);        System.out.println(age >= 18 && age < 65);    }}
Outputfalse
true
true
true

&& needs both true, || needs at least one, ! flips.
frames.ask: In a && b, if a is false, is b even looked at?

frames.check: No, and that is the fourth surprise.
frames.teach: && and || short circuit: they stop as soon as the answer is certain. That is not a curiosity, it is a technique. It lets you write if (n != 0 && total / n > 5) safely, because when n is zero the division never happens.
frames.ask: Finally, precedence. What is 2 + 3 * 4?

frames.teach: The order is: brackets, then unary (++ -- ! and casts), then * / %, then + -, then the comparisons, then &&, then ||, then = last of all. Use brackets freely. They cost nothing and they show the examiner what you meant.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
SurpriseWhat happensThe fix or the rule
Integer division7 / 2 is 3; the remainder is droppedcast one side: (double) sum / count
+ is two operatorswith any String on either side it joins, otherwise it adds, left to rightbracket the arithmetic: "n = " + (a + b)
a++ against ++apost uses the old value then adds; pre adds then uses the new oneonly matters when the value is used in the same expression
Short circuit&& stops at the first false, || at the first trueput the guard on the left: n != 0 && x / n > 5

Precedence, highest first: brackets, unary and casts, * / %, + -, relational, == and !=, &&, ||, then assignment.

And % earns its keep: n % 2 == 0 tests even, n % 10 gives the last digit, n /= 10 removes it. Those two together are how every digit question on this paper is solved.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. What are 17 / 5 and 17 % 5?

2. Write the line that prints the average of int sum over int n, correctly.

3. int a = 3; then System.out.println(a++ + " " + a); prints what?

4. What does System.out.println("x" + 1 + 2); print?
blocks.answer: 1. 3 and 2. 2. System.out.println((double) sum / n); 3. 3 4: the post increment uses 3, then a is 4 by the time the second part is evaluated. 4. x12; the leftmost + already has text on its left, so both join.

blocks.big:
Two ints divide as ints. A String next to plus makes it glue. Post uses then
adds. And-and stops at the first false.
blocks.sub: In a dry run, write the value of every sub-expression above the line before you combine them. Never evaluate a whole line in your head.

title: Reading Input, Printing It Back Neatly
lead:
Two of the three long questions on the last paper said "using JOptionPane
only, for all input and output". If you cannot write those two lines from memory you cannot
start those questions, so this short lesson is worth more than its length.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Read a value from the user with Scanner and with JOptionPane, convert what a dialog gives you into a number, and print a result to a stated number of decimal places with printf.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: There are two ways in, and the paper names which it wants. The first is the console reader, Scanner. It needs an import at the very top of the file, above the class.
frames.ask:
Which package do you think it comes
from?

frames.teach:
so the line is import java.util.Scanner;. Then you make one, pointed at the keyboard.

import java.util.Scanner;public class ReadIn {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        System.out.print("Name: ");        String name = in.nextLine();        System.out.print("Score: ");        int score = in.nextInt();        System.out.println(name + " scored " + score);    }}
OutputName: Score: Ada scored 72

Read the shape: import, create, then a next... call per value.
frames.ask: There are three different next calls in play. What do you think nextInt(), nextDouble() and nextLine() each return?

frames.check: An int, a double and a String.
frames.teach: That is the whole API and you must have it cold: nextInt, nextDouble, next for one word, nextLine for a whole line, and nextBoolean. Ask for the type you want and Scanner converts for you.
frames.ask:
Now the other way in. The paper often demands JOptionPane. Which package is
that from?

frames.teach:
note the x: import javax.swing.JOptionPane;. It is the pop-up window version, and it behaves differently from Scanner in the one way that costs marks.

import javax.swing.JOptionPane;public class Popup {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String text = JOptionPane.showInputDialog("Enter your score:");        int score = Integer.parseInt(text);   // the dialog gives text        JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "You scored " + score);        System.exit(0);                           // closes the program    }}
frames.ask: Look at the second line of main. Why is Integer.parseInt needed there when Scanner needed nothing?

frames.check: Because a dialog can only ever hand back text.
frames.teach: showInputDialog returns a String, always, even when the user typed 42. So you must convert it yourself: Integer.parseInt(text) for a whole number, Double.parseDouble(text) for a decimal. Forgetting that conversion is the single most common JOptionPane error in an exam script.
frames.ask: What is the matching call for showing a message?

frames.teach: The null is the parent window, and there is not one, so it is always null. And finish with System.exit(0);, because a window program does not stop on its own when main ends.
Now out. You know println and print. The third is printf, which exists for one reason: controlling how a number looks.
frames.ask: A total comes out as 10547.7868 and the question says two decimal places. What does println give you?

frames.teach:
printf takes a format string full of placeholders, then the values to drop into them.

public class Printf {    public static void main(String[] args) {        double total = 10547.7868;        System.out.println(total);        System.out.printf("%.2f%n", total);        System.out.printf("%-10s%8.2f%n", "Total", total);        System.out.printf("%d items at %.2f each%n", 3, 19.5);    }}
Output10547.7868
10547.79
Total     10547.79
3 items at 19.50 each

title: The Dry Run: Being the Computer, on Paper
lead:
Question One of the last paper gave you a program and said: state the five
outputs. Ten marks, no writing required, no creativity. It is the single most reliable
block of marks on the paper, and this is the only technique it needs.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Take any program you are handed, trace it line by line with a table of every variable, and state exactly what it prints and in what order, without a computer.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: The method is a table. One column per variable, one row per pass through the code, and a column on the right for anything printed. You fill it in by being stupid on purpose: do exactly what the line says, write the result down, move to the next line.
frames.ask: Why write it down rather than keep it in your head?

frames.check: Because your head silently skips steps
frames.teach:
, and the whole point of the exercise is that the machine does not. Here is a small one to practise on. 

public class Trace {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int total = 0;        for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {            total = total + i;            System.out.println("i=" + i + " total=" + total);        }        System.out.println("Final " + total);    }}
frames.ask: Do not read past it. Draw the table now: columns for i, total, and printed.

frames.check: Here is the table you should have drawn.
frames.teach:

333 + 3 = 6i=3 total=6
446 + 4 = 10i=4 total=10

Outputi=1 total=1

frames.ask: Why is there a row where i is 5 but nothing was printed?

frames.check: Because the test is made BEFORE the body runs.
frames.teach: i becomes 5, 5 <= 4 is false, and the loop ends without executing anything. Always write that last row. It is where off-by-one answers come from, and the examiner knows it.
frames.ask: How many lines of output are there in total?

frames.check: Five: four from inside the loop and one after it.
frames.teach:
Counting the output lines before you write them is a free check, because the question usually
tells you how many there should be. On the last paper it said "state the five outputs", which
tells you the array has five entries and the loop runs five times.

Now the paper's own question, shortened to three numbers so it fits here. It decides whether a number is an Armstrong number: one that equals the sum of its own digits, each raised to the power of how many digits there are. 153 is one, because 1³ + 5³ + 3³ = 153. 

public class Armstrong {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372};        for (int idx = 0; idx < numbers.length; idx++) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            while (temp > 0) { digits++; temp /= 10; }            temp = n;            while (temp > 0) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                for (int p = 0; p < digits; p++) power *= d;                sum += power;                temp /= 10;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));        }    }}
frames.ask:
Read the program and find the two
things the first while loop is for.

frames.check:
It counts the digits, and it destroys temp doing
it.
frames.teach: temp /= 10 chops a digit off the right each time, by integer division, until nothing is left. That is why temp = n; appears again afterwards: the counter used temp up and it has to be put back.
frames.ask: For n = 370, what is digits after that first loop?

frames.teach: 370 to 37 to 3 to 0, three steps. Now the second loop, which does the real work. temp % 10 takes the last digit, the inner for multiplies it by itself digits times, and temp /= 10 throws that digit away.
frames.ask:
Trace 370. Write the three digits it pulls off, in order, and their
cubes.

frames.teach:
ndigitsdigits pulled off, and their powerssumprinted

Output370 -> ARMSTRONG

frames.ask: 372 gave 378. What single thing decided the answer?

frames.check: The comparison sum == n at the end.
frames.teach: That is what the ? : is doing: it is a compact if-else, called the ternary operator. test ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Read it as an if-else and it stops being strange.
frames.ask:
The real paper had five numbers, adding
407 and 408. Work those two out now, on paper.

frames.teach:
If you got both, you can answer that ten mark question. The
whole technique was: a table, one row per number, and doing exactly what each line says.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
1. Draw the table first. One column per variable, one for what is printed. Do it before you read the code properly.
  2. Write the starting value of every variable, including the ones set to 0.
  3. Take one line at a time and do exactly what it says. No shortcuts, no "obviously this just".
  4. At a loop, write the test out and answer it before you enter the body, every pass. Include the pass that fails, so you can see why it stopped.
  5. Add a row to the printed column the moment a print executes, not at the end. Order is part of the answer.
  6. Count your output lines against what the question expects. If it says five and you have four, you dropped a pass.

Two idioms you will meet in every one of these: n % 10 is the last digit and n /= 10 removes it, so a while (n > 0) loop around those two walks a number digit by digit, right to left. And test ? a : b is an if-else squeezed into an expression.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Forgetting that a counting loop destroys its counter. That is why the program resets temp = n. If you trace with the used-up value you get zero for everything.
  • Tracing in your head. Four passes is where it stops working, and the exam gives you five.
  • Missing the final pass. The one where the test fails still happens, and for <= against < it decides the answer.
  • Not reading what is printed literally. If the code prints "i=" + i, the answer is i=1, not 1. The examiner marks the string you wrote.

3. Rewrite x = (a > b) ? a : b; as an if-else.

4. Trace int t = 0; for (int i = 5; i > 0; i -= 2) t += i; and give t.
blocks.answer: 1. 7 and 40. 2. Five times, i is 5 at the end. 3. if (a > b) { x = a; } else { x = b; } 4. i takes 5, 3, 1, so t is 9.

blocks.big:
A table, one row per pass, and do exactly what the line says. Write the pass
that fails the test too.
blocks.sub: Ten marks on the last paper for this and nothing else. It is the most reliable question on the paper and it needs no invention at all.

title: if, if-else and the Ladder
lead:
Section C of the last paper said, in as many words, "use nested if-else
statements, not a switch, and not independent or separate if checks". The examiner is telling
you he can tell the difference, and marking it.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write an if, an if-else and a full ladder; say which branch runs for any given input; and write nested if-else logic when the paper demands it rather than a chain of separate ifs.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: An if takes a condition in brackets, and runs its block only when that condition is true. An else catches everything else and takes no condition of its own. When you have more than two outcomes you chain them: else if, as many times as you need, and that chain is called a ladder.
frames.ask:
In a ladder of one if, three else-ifs and an else, how many blocks
run?

frames.teach:
Java tests from the top and stops at the first condition that is true, skipping every test below it. That single fact is the whole of the grading question. Here is the school's scheme.

public class Grade {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int score = 64;        char grade;        if (score >= 70) {            grade = 'A';        } else if (score >= 60) {            grade = 'B';        } else if (score >= 50) {            grade = 'C';        } else if (score >= 45) {            grade = 'D';        } else {            grade = 'F';        }        System.out.println("Grade: " + grade);    }}
OutputGrade: B
frames.ask: Look at the second test, score >= 60. Why does it not also need to check that the score is under 70?

frames.check:
Because anything 70 or over already matched the line
above and never reached here.
frames.teach:
The ladder carries that knowledge for you. It follows that the ORDER is not cosmetic. Watch what happens upside down.

public class BadLadder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int score = 95;        char grade;        if (score >= 45) {            grade = 'D';        } else if (score >= 50) {            grade = 'C';        } else if (score >= 70) {            grade = 'A';        } else {            grade = 'F';        }        System.out.println("Grade: " + grade);    }}
OutputGrade: D

A 95 comes out as a D.
frames.ask:
State the rule that stops this
happening.

frames.check:
Order a ladder from the most demanding condition to the
least.
frames.teach:
Highest band first, then down. That, or give every branch both bounds
explicitly, which is more writing and more to get wrong.
frames.ask: What would happen if you wrote four separate if statements instead of a ladder?

frames.check:
All four would be tested, and more than one could
run.
frames.teach: The last one to match would overwrite the earlier answers, so a 95 would end up a D again. Separate ifs are not a ladder, and the paper says so explicitly.

Now nested if-else: an if inside another if, used when the second question only makes sense once the first is answered. The paper's ticket question is exactly this shape: what tier are you, and then, given that tier, how many days. 

public class Nested {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String tier = "Gold";        int days = 3;        int discount;        if (tier.equals("Gold")) {            if (days == 3) {                discount = 25;            } else {                discount = 15;            }        } else {            if (days == 3) {                discount = 10;            } else {                discount = 5;            }        }        System.out.println("Discount " + discount + "%");    }}
frames.ask:
Read it and say what decides which of the four discounts is
reached.

frames.check:
The outer test picks a pair, the inner test picks one of
that pair.
frames.teach:
OutputDiscount 25%

Two conditions, four outcomes, and every path ends in exactly one assignment.
frames.ask: How do you tell which if an else belongs to?

frames.check:
By its braces, and failing that by its
indentation.
frames.teach: An else attaches to the nearest unmatched if. That is why you should always write the braces even for a single statement: without them, an else can silently attach to the wrong if, and the program compiles and quietly does the wrong thing.
frames.ask: So what is the habit?

frames.check: Braces on every if and every else, always.
frames.teach:
It
costs two characters and removes a whole family of errors. Now validation, which the paper
asks for in nearly every long question: reject a score outside 0 to 100.
frames.ask: Write that test two ways, one with && and one with ||.

frames.teach: Use whichever reads more naturally for what you want to do next. And note that Java has no 0 <= score <= 100; you must write both comparisons and join them.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
if (condition) {                    <- runs only when true    ...}if (condition) {                    <- one block or the other, never both    ...} else {    ...}if (highest) {                      <- the LADDER: first true wins, rest skipped    ...} else if (next highest) {    ...} else {                          <- everything left over, no condition    ...}

The grading pattern, as a shape: test the highest band first, use else if for every band after it, and finish with a bare else. Never repeat an upper bound you have already excluded, and never use separate ifs.

The three control structures, if the paper asks you to compare them: sequence is statements carried out one after another in the order written; selection chooses between alternatives so that only one runs, with if and switch; iteration repeats a block, with for, while and do-while.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• A ladder in ascending order. Everyone gets the lowest grade, silently.
  • Separate ifs where a ladder was asked for. The paper names the structure it wants; using another one loses marks even when the answer comes out right.
  • A semicolon after the condition: if (x > 5); is a complete, empty if, and the block after it runs unconditionally. It compiles.
  • Omitting braces on a nested if. The else attaches to the wrong if.
  • Comparing Strings with ==. In tier.equals("Gold") that equals is not optional. Lesson 2.9 explains why.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. In a ladder, how many blocks run, and which?

2. Write the five band grading ladder from A to F on paper, from memory.

3. What is wrong with if (score > 100);?

4. Write the validation test that accepts a score from 0 to 100 inclusive.
blocks.answer: 1. Exactly one, the first whose condition is true. 2. Descending: 70 A, 60 B, 50 C, 45 D, else F. 3. The semicolon ends the if, so the block that follows always runs. 4. if (score >= 0 && score <= 100).

blocks.big:
Highest band first. The ladder stops at the first true, so every later test
already knows what came before it.
blocks.sub: Braces on every branch, even the one line ones. That is what keeps an else attached to the if you meant.

title: switch, and the Fall-Through Trap
lead:
Question Five of the last paper said "use a switch statement to return a base
ticket price for Day 1, Day 2, or Day 3". Named structure again, so it has to be a switch, and
the missing break is the error he plants in it.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write a switch statement that returns a different value for each case; say exactly what a missing break does; group cases that share an answer; and say when a switch is the right choice and when it is not allowed.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A switch takes one value and jumps to the case that matches it. It is the right tool when you are comparing one variable against a list of exact values, and a ladder is right when you are testing ranges.
frames.ask: Grading by score band: switch or ladder?

frames.teach:
because a band is a range and a case must be an exact value. Day number to price is the switch shape.

public class Ticket {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int day = 2;        double price;        switch (day) {            case 1:                price = 75.0;                break;            case 2:                price = 60.0;                break;            case 3:                price = 45.0;                break;            default:                price = 0.0;        }        System.out.println("Price " + price);    }}
OutputPrice 60.0

Read the anatomy: switch (value), then case X: for each exact match, then default: for anything else.
frames.ask: What is the break at the end of each case for?

frames.teach:
And here is the whole trap: without it, Java does not stop at the end of a case. It carries straight on into the next one, and the next, until it hits a break or the closing brace. That is called fall-through. 

public class Fall {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int day = 1;        switch (day) {            case 1:                System.out.println("one");            case 2:                System.out.println("two");            case 3:                System.out.println("three");                break;            case 4:                System.out.println("four");        }    }}
frames.ask:
Predict what this prints for day = 1. Be
careful.

frames.teach:
Outputone
two
three

It matched case 1, printed, fell into case 2, printed, fell into case 3, printed, and only then met a break. Case 4 was never reached.
frames.ask: So how many breaks does a five case switch need?

frames.check: One at the end of every case,
frames.teach:
including, by habit,
the last one and the default. The last does not strictly need it, but writing it means you
never forget when you add a case underneath.

Fall-through is not always a bug. Left deliberately, it is how you make several values share one answer. 

public class Season {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int month = 7;        String season;        switch (month) {            case 12: case 1: case 2:                season = "Harmattan";                break;            case 6: case 7: case 8:                season = "Rainy";                break;            default:                season = "Other";        }        System.out.println(season);    }}
frames.ask:
Read this and say which months give
Rainy.

frames.teach:
OutputRainy

Cases 6 and 7 have no statements at all, so they fall into case 8, which does the work and breaks. That is the intended use, and it reads clearly because the empty cases sit on one line.
frames.ask: What does default do if you leave it out and nothing matches?

frames.teach: and the variable keeps whatever it had. Always write a default, even if it only throws an error or sets a safe value. The paper's ticket question says an invalid day should throw an IllegalArgumentException, and the default is where that goes: default: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Day must be 1, 2 or 3");
frames.ask: Which types may a switch switch on?

frames.check: Whole number types, char, String and enum.
frames.teach: byte, short, int, char, String and enums. Not double and not boolean, which is a favourite objective question: you cannot switch on a price, only on something exactly comparable.
frames.ask: Last one. Why must every case label be a constant?

frames.check:
Because the compiler builds the jump table before the
program runs.
frames.teach: case n: where n is a variable will not compile; case 3: and case MAX: where MAX is final both will.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The shape, and the four rules
blocks.html:
switch (value) {                  <- one value, exact matches only    case 1:        ...        break;                    <- or it falls into case 2    case 2: case 3:                <- deliberate sharing: 2 falls into 3        ...        break;    default:                       <- everything else. Always write one        ...}
  • A missing break falls through into the next case and keeps going until it meets one.
  • Switch on: byte, short, int, char, String, enum. Not double, not boolean.
  • Every case label must be a constant, a literal or a final.
  • Switch for exact values, ladder for ranges. Say that sentence if asked to compare them.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. A switch has cases 1, 2, 3 with no breaks at all, and the value is 2. Which cases run?

2. Can you switch on a double? On a String?

3. Write the default that rejects an invalid day with an exception.

4. When would you choose a ladder over a switch?
blocks.answer: 1. Cases 2 and 3, in that order. 2. No to double, yes to String. 3. default: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Day must be 1, 2 or 3"); 4. Whenever the test is a range or any condition more complex than an exact match.

blocks.big:
One value, exact cases, break at the end of every one. No break means it runs
straight on into the next case.
blocks.sub: Switch for exact values, ladder for ranges. And always write a default, even when nothing should reach it.

title: The Three Loops
lead:
Every question on this paper contains a loop. Learn the three shapes as
shapes, so that under pressure you write the skeleton first and fill it in, rather than
inventing it line by line.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write a for, a while and a do-while loop; say how many times each runs; choose the right one for a stated job; and trace a nested loop by hand.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A for loop puts all three moving parts on one line: start; test; step, separated by semicolons. for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) means start at one, keep going while i is at most three, add one each time.
frames.ask:
In what order do those three run? Say it
before you look.

frames.check:
Start once. Then test, body, step, test, body, step, and
so on.
frames.teach:
The test happens before each body, and the step happens after it. Here are all three loops doing the same job.

public class Loops {    public static void main(String[] args) {        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {            System.out.print(i + " ");        }        System.out.println();        int j = 1;        while (j <= 3) {            System.out.print(j + " ");            j++;        }        System.out.println();        int k = 1;        do {            System.out.print(k + " ");            k++;        } while (k <= 3);        System.out.println();    }}
Output1 2 3 
1 2 3 
1 2 3
frames.ask:
All three printed the same thing. What is actually different about
them?

frames.teach: The for gathers them on one line. The while scatters them: start above, test in the brackets, step at the bottom of the body. The do-while is the while with its test moved to the end.
frames.ask:
And that last move changes one thing.
What?

frames.check: A do-while always runs at least once.
frames.teach:
Its test comes after the body, so the body has already happened before anything is checked. Proof:

public class AtLeastOnce {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int n = 100;        while (n < 10) {            System.out.println("the while body never ran");        }        do {            System.out.println("the do body ran anyway");        } while (n < 10);    }}
Outputthe do body ran anyway

The while body never ran; the do body ran once even though the condition was false all along.
frames.ask:
Which loop would you use to keep asking for a password until it is
right?

frames.teach: because you must ask at least once before you can possibly know. That is the classic use, and the note it ends with is worth copying: a do-while ends with a semicolon after the condition, which no other loop does.

Now the paper's own multiplication table, which asks for it
"in a neatly formatted manner".
frames.ask:
What must the for loop's test be to include
12?

frames.teach:
not i < 12, which would stop at 11.

public class Table {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int n = 7;        for (int i = 1; i <= 12; i++) {            System.out.printf("%2d x %2d = %3d%n", n, i, n * i);        }    }}
Output 7 x  1 =   7

 7 x  3 =  21

 7 x  7 =  49
 7 x  8 =  56
 7 x  9 =  63
 7 x 10 =  70
