 7 x 12 =  84

The printf is what makes it neat: %2d and %3d pad each number to a fixed width, so the columns line up.
frames.ask: How many lines did that print?

frames.teach: A count-controlled loop runs last minus first plus one times when the test is <=. Getting that count right before you write anything is the cheapest error check there is.
frames.ask:
Now a nested loop. If the outer runs 3 times and the inner runs 2, how many
times does the inner body run in total?

frames.teach:
The inner loop runs completely, from its own start, on every single pass of the outer one.

public class Grid {    public static void main(String[] args) {        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {            for (int j = 1; j <= 2; j++) {                System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");            }            System.out.println();        }    }}
Output11 12 
21 22 
31 32
frames.ask: Why did the output break into three lines rather than one?

frames.check: The println() sits in the OUTER loop,
frames.teach:
after the inner loop has finished. That placement is the whole difference between a row of
output and a grid of it, and in a dry run it is the thing to check first: which loop is each
statement inside?

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The three shapes, and when to use each
blocks.html:
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {      <- start; test; step, all on one line    ...}int i = 1;                          <- start, abovewhile (i <= n) {                    <- test, before each pass    ...    i++;                            <- step, at the bottom. NEVER forget it}int i = 1;do {                                <- body first, so it always runs once    ...    i++;} while (i <= n);                  <- test at the end, and a semicolon
UseWhenCalled
foryou know how many times before you start, or you are walking an arraycount controlled
whileyou must keep going until something happens, and it might not happen at allcondition controlled
do-whilethe same, but the body must happen at least onceexit controlled

The accumulator pattern, which the paper wants every year: declare total and count and set them to 0 before the loop; do total += x; and count++; inside it; print them after it. Three places, and getting one wrong is the commonest loop error there is.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Forgetting the step in a while loop. The condition never changes and the program hangs for ever. This is planted in find-the-errors questions.
  • < where <= was meant. One pass short, every time. For a table to 12 you need i <= 12.
  • Declaring the total inside the loop. It resets on every pass and the answer is always the last value.
  • A semicolon after the for line: for (...); is a complete empty loop, and the block after it runs once.
  • Using i after the loop. A variable declared in the for header does not exist outside it.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) run, and what is i afterwards?

2. Which loop is guaranteed to run at least once, and why?

3. Outer loop 4 passes, inner loop 5. How many times does the inner body run?

4. Write, on paper, the accumulator that totals an array of ints.
blocks.answer: 1. Five times; i is 5, and only inside the loop's own scope. 2. do-while, because the test comes after the body. 3. Twenty. 4. int sum = 0; then for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { sum += a[i]; } then print sum.

blocks.big:
Start, test, step. for gathers them, while scatters them, do-while moves the
test to the end and runs once regardless.
blocks.sub: Zero it before, add inside, print after. Three places, and every accumulating question on the paper is those three lines.

title: Turning a for into a while, and Back
lead:
This has its own lesson because it has its own marks. Question One of the
2025/2026 paper said: "Retain other things but change the For Loop to While loop and the
While loops to For loops." That is half of a ten mark part, for a mechanical translation you
can learn in twenty minutes.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Take any for loop and rewrite it as a while loop that does exactly the same thing, and take any while loop and rewrite it as a for, without changing a single value the program produces.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Both loops have the same three moving parts. A for puts them on one line; a while puts them in three different places. So the conversion is not a rewrite at all, it is moving three pieces to three known homes.
frames.ask: Name the three parts of for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++).

frames.teach:
Here they are again with their destinations, and this table is the whole lesson.

PartIn the forGoes where in the while
Startfirst slot, int i = 1on its own line, above the loop
Testmiddle slot, i <= 5unchanged, in the while brackets
Steplast slot, i++the last line inside the body
frames.ask: Which of the three is the one people forget?

frames.teach:
It is the one that changes homes most dramatically, and if you leave it out the loop never ends. Here is a for loop.

public class ForVer {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int total = 0;        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {            total += i;        }        System.out.println("Total " + total);    }}
OutputTotal 15
frames.ask: Now write its while version on paper, before you look.

frames.check: Here it is, with the three parts labelled.
frames.teach:
public class WhileVer {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int total = 0;        int i = 1;              // 1. the start, lifted out and above        while (i <= 5) {        // 2. the test, unchanged            total += i;            i++;                // 3. the step, moved to the bottom        }        System.out.println("Total " + total);    }}
OutputTotal 15

Total 15 both times. That is the check: convert, then confirm the output is identical.
frames.ask: What goes wrong if the step is left out?

frames.check: i stays 1 for ever and the loop never ends.
frames.teach:
int total = 0;int i = 1;while (i <= 5) {    total += i;          <- the step is missing, so i is always 1}

Nothing here is worth running, and nothing here would ever stop. That is why the step is the first thing to check in your answer and the first thing to look for when the paper asks you to find the errors.
frames.ask:
Now the other direction. What is different about
the scope of i in the two versions?

frames.check:
In the for it exists only inside the loop; in the while
it outlives the loop.
frames.ask: So how do you convert a while back into a for?

frames.teach: Take the line above the loop and put it in the first slot; take the condition and put it in the second; find the line at the bottom of the body that changes the counter and put it in the third. Then delete both original lines: leaving the step behind inside the body as well as in the header double-steps the counter, and that is the classic half-converted answer.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
// FOR                            // the same loop as a WHILEfor (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {       int i = 1;          // 1 start, above    total += i;                    while (i <= 5) {   // 2 test, unchanged}                                      total += i;                                       i++;         // 3 step, at the bottom                                   }

The four step checklist, to write in the margin before you convert:

  1. Start comes out of the header and goes on its own line above the loop.
  2. Test moves across unchanged, into the while brackets.
  3. Step goes to the last line inside the body.
  4. Check the output is identical. Same numbers, same count of lines, same order.

Going the other way, do the same four in reverse, and delete the two lines you moved from rather than leaving copies behind.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• The step left out entirely. Infinite loop. The commonest of the three.
  • The step left in the body AND put in the header. The counter goes up twice a pass, so the loop runs half as many times and the total is wrong.
  • The start left inside the loop. It resets the counter every pass, so the loop never ends either.
  • And one more: if the body contains a continue, moving the step to the bottom of the body changes the meaning, because continue skips it. In a for loop the step still happens. Convert those with care, and say so in your answer.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Convert for (int k = 10; k > 0; k -= 2) sum += k; to a while loop.

2. Convert this to a for loop: int n = 1; while (n < 100) { n *= 2; }

3. What are the three homes the three parts move to?

4. Why can a continue in the body break a conversion?
blocks.answer: 1. int k = 10; then while (k > 0) { sum += k; k -= 2; } 2. for (int n = 1; n < 100; n *= 2) { }, with the body now empty. 3. Start above the loop, test in the brackets, step at the bottom of the body. 4. Because continue jumps past the rest of the body, which in the while version now includes the step, so the counter stops advancing.

blocks.big:
Start goes above. Test stays put. Step goes to the bottom of the body. Then
check the output is identical.
blocks.sub: Ten marks on the last paper included this conversion. Practise it on three loops tonight and it becomes free.

blocks.label: Now prove it
blocks.tag: every objective question on this topic

title: break and continue
lead:
Both find-the-errors questions on the last paper were this pattern with one
piece sabotaged. Learn the pattern properly and you are not spotting errors, you are
comparing what is there against what you know it should be.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Use break and continue correctly, say exactly which loop each one acts on inside a nested loop, and write the "process some, skip some, stop after N" pattern that Section A of the paper is built from.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Two words, and they are easy to confuse because they both jump. break leaves the loop entirely. continue abandons this pass and starts the next one.
frames.ask:
So which one would you use to skip an item you do not want to
process?

frames.teach:
And break for "I have found what I came for" or "I have done enough". 

public class Escape {    public static void main(String[] args) {        for (int n = 1; n <= 9; n++) {            if (n == 4) {                continue;            }            if (n == 7) {                break;            }            System.out.print(n + " ");        }        System.out.println();    }}
frames.ask: Predict the output of this before you read on.

frames.teach:
Output1 2 3 5 6

4 was skipped by continue, so nothing printed for it but the loop carried on. At 7 the break ended everything, so 7, 8 and 9 never happened.
frames.ask: In a for loop, does continue still run the step, i++?

frames.teach: That is important: continue in a for loop jumps to the step, then the test. In a while loop it jumps straight to the test, so if your step is at the bottom of the body it gets skipped and the loop hangs. That is the trap in Lesson 2.4's conversion warning, and it is worth a mark to notice.
frames.ask: Now nesting. In two loops, one inside the other, which loop does a break leave?

frames.check: Only the innermost one it is inside.
frames.teach:
The outer loop carries on as if nothing happened.

public class Inner {    public static void main(String[] args) {        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {            for (int j = 1; j <= 3; j++) {                if (j == 2) {                    break;                }                System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");            }        }        System.out.println();    }}
Output11 21 31

Three outer passes each printed one value, because the inner loop broke at j = 2 every time.
frames.ask: So how do you leave BOTH loops at once?

frames.teach: Set a boolean stop = false; outside, set it true when you want out, and add && !stop to the outer loop's condition. That is exactly the shape the 2025/2026 paper's Question One uses, which is why it declares boolean stop = false; at the top.

Now the pattern itself, because both Section A questions are it. In words: walk a list, skip the ones that do not qualify, do something with the ones that do, count them, and stop once you have enough.
frames.ask: Which of break and continue does each of those three jobs?

frames.check:
continue skips, break stops, and a counter does the
counting.
frames.teach:
Here is the paper's discount question, faithfully.

public class Discount {    public static void main(String[] args) {        double[] prices = {15.5, 42.0, 8.75, 60.0, 33.25, 90.0};        double total = 0;        int count = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < prices.length; i++) {            if (prices[i] < 20) {                continue;            }            total += prices[i] * 0.9;            count++;            if (count == 4) {                break;            }        }        System.out.println("Total: " + total + "  Count: " + count);    }}
OutputTotal: 202.72500000000002  Count: 4
frames.ask:
Read the output carefully against what the paper says the answer should
be: Total: 202.725 Count: 4.

frames.check:
The count matches. The total ends in
...00000000002.
frames.teach: That is not a bug in the program, it is how double works: a binary fraction cannot represent 0.9 exactly, and the tiny error shows when you print the raw value. The fix is to format the output, not to change the arithmetic.
frames.ask: Which call would print it as 202.725?

frames.teach: Remember that for any money answer on this paper: compute in double, print with printf and a stated number of decimal places. Writing "Total: " + total is what produces the long tail, and the examiner's expected answer never has one.
frames.ask: Last one. Where must count++ sit relative to the continue?

frames.teach: Anything above the continue runs for every item, including the ones you meant to skip. Order inside the body is the whole meaning of this pattern: test and skip first, then process, then count, then test whether to stop.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The Section A pattern, in order
blocks.html:
double total = 0;                     // accumulators BEFORE the loopint count = 0;for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {   // walk every item    if (not wanted) {        continue;                   // 1. skip, and go to the next    }    total += ...;                    // 2. process the ones that qualify    count++;                         // 3. count it, AFTER the skip    if (count == n) {        break;                      // 4. enough: leave the loop    }}
  • break leaves the loop it is in. continue abandons this pass and goes to the next.
  • Both act on the innermost loop only. To leave two, use a boolean flag in the outer condition.
  • In a for loop, continue still runs the step. In a while loop it does not, so a step at the bottom of the body is skipped.
  • Money is printed with printf and %.2f, never concatenated raw.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. What does for (int i=1;i<=5;i++){ if(i==3) continue; System.out.print(i);} print?

2. And with break instead of continue?

3. How do you leave both loops of a nested pair?

4. Why does "Total: " + 202.725 sometimes print a long tail, and what do you write instead?
blocks.answer: 1. 1245. 2. 12. 3. A boolean flag set inside and tested in the outer loop's condition. 4. Because a double cannot hold some decimals exactly; use printf("%.3f", total).

blocks.big:
continue skips one, break stops them all, and both only ever act on the loop
they are standing in.
blocks.sub: Skip first, then process, then count, then decide whether to stop. That order is the pattern, and both Section A questions are it.

title: Methods: void, Value Returning, Parameters
lead:
Section B and Section C both say "create a method that returns...". When the
paper names a method and says it returns something, printing the answer instead of returning
it loses the mark however right the number is.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write a void method and a value returning method, call each correctly, tell a parameter from an argument, and say what parameter passing actually does to the caller's variables.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A method is a named block you write once and call as often as you like. Its first line, the header, has four parts in a fixed order: public static, then what it gives back, then its name, then what it takes in, in brackets.
frames.ask: In public static int cube(int num), which part says what it gives back?

frames.teach:
That is the return type, and it is the single most important word in the header. If it says int, the method must hand back an int. Here is one that hands back nothing.

public class Greeter {    public static void greet(String name) {        System.out.println("Hello, " + name);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        greet("Ada");        greet("Victor");    }}
OutputHello, Ada
Hello, Victor

void means exactly that: no value comes back.
frames.ask: What is the name for that kind of method?

frames.teach:
It performs an action, in this case printing, and that is its whole purpose. The other kind computes something and gives it back with return. 

public class Cube {    public static int cube(int num) {        return num * num * num;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int result = cube(4);        System.out.println(result);        System.out.println(cube(2) + cube(3));    }}
frames.ask: Read this and write the statement that puts cube(4) into a variable called result.

frames.teach:
Output64
35

Because it returns a value, a call to it is a value: you can assign it, print it, or add two of them together, which is why cube(2) + cube(3) works.
frames.ask: Could you write greet("Ada") + 1 with the void method from before?

frames.teach:
There is nothing to add. A void call is a statement, not a value, and using it as one will not compile. Here is the difference made visible.

public class Both {    public static void show(int n) {        System.out.println("the number is " + n);    }    public static int doubled(int n) {        return n * 2;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        show(5);        int answer = doubled(5);        System.out.println("doubled returned " + answer);    }}
Outputthe number is 5
doubled returned 10
frames.ask: Give the one sentence that distinguishes the two kinds.

frames.check: A void method performs an action and returns no value; a value returning method computes a result and hands it back with return.
frames.teach: Learn that sentence; it is asked directly, and it is worth marks on its own.
Two words the paper distinguishes. In the header, int num is a parameter: a name for a value that will arrive. At the call, cube(4), the 4 is an argument: the actual value handed over.
frames.ask: Which is which in area(width, 3.0) called against area(double w, double h)?

frames.check: w and h are parameters; width and 3.0 are arguments.
frames.teach: Now the question the paper actually asks: what does passing an argument DO? Java has one answer, pass by value, and it means a copy is handed over.
frames.ask:
So if a method changes its parameter, does the caller's variable
change?

frames.teach:
The method got a copy, and it changed the copy. But there is a twist, and it is the whole of the marks here.

public class Pass {    public static void change(int n, int[] row) {        n = 99;        row[0] = 99;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int number = 1;        int[] values = {1, 2, 3};        change(number, values);        System.out.println("number is still " + number);        System.out.println("values[0] is now " + values[0]);    }}
Outputnumber is still 1
values[0] is now 99
frames.ask:
The int did not change but the array did. Why, if both were passed the
same way?

frames.check:
Because what is copied for an array is the
reference, not the contents.
frames.teach: Java always passes by value, but for an object the value it copies is the arrow pointing at the object. Both arrows now point at the same array, so a change through one is visible through the other. Say it exactly like that: Java is always pass by value, and for objects the value passed is a reference.
frames.ask: What does that mean for a method that must change an array?

frames.check:
It can, and it does not need to return
anything.
frames.teach: A method that sorts or fills an array can be void. A method that must give back a number, a count or a String has to return it, and its return type must say so.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The header, and the four distinctions
blocks.html:
public static   int    cube   (int num)   {//               ^type   ^name   ^parameters    return num * num * num;   // must give back an int}
PairThe differenceExample
void vs value returningvoid performs an action and returns nothing; value returning computes a result and hands it backprintln against cube
parameter vs argumentthe parameter is the name in the header; the argument is the value supplied at the callint num against cube(4)
built in vs user definedbuilt in comes with Java and needs no definition; user defined is one you writeMath.sqrt against cube
pass by valueJava always copies the value. For an object, the value copied is the reference, so the object itself can be changedsee the listing above

Five benefits of using methods, if asked: reusability, readability, easier testing and debugging, easier maintenance because a change is made in one place, and the ability to split a large problem between people.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Printing where the paper said return. "Create a method that returns the total" means return total;. A println earns nothing.
  • A value returning method with a path that returns nothing. Every route out must return, including the one after the loop. Java will refuse to compile it.
  • Using the paper's name loosely. When it names the method and its parameters, copy them exactly: display_achievement_summary style names are marked.
  • Forgetting static. A method called from main without an object must be static, or it will not compile.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Write the header of a method that takes an int array and gives back an int.

2. What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?

3. A method changes its int parameter. Does the caller see it? What if it is an array?

4. Why must a method called from main be static?
blocks.answer: 1. public static int total(int[] a) { 2. The parameter is the name in the header, the argument is the value passed at the call. 3. No for the int; yes for the array, because the reference was copied and both point at the same object. 4. Because main is static and no object of the class exists yet.

blocks.big:
public static, return type, name, parameters. void acts, a return type
computes. Java copies the value, and for an object the value is the arrow.
blocks.sub: If the question says returns, write return. That single word is the difference between full marks and none on those parts.

blocks.label: Now prove it
blocks.tag: every objective question on this topic

title: Overloading, static, and the Method Signature
lead: Question One part A of the last paper: "Define method overloading in Java, and state precisely the role that the method signature plays in enabling the compiler to resolve an overloaded call at compile time." Two marks, and the word precisely means he wants the signature named exactly.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Define method overloading and state precisely what the method signature is and how the compiler uses it to choose between overloaded methods; and tell a static method from an instance method.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Overloading is writing several methods with the same name in the same class, which do the same kind of job for different inputs. You have used it already: println takes an int, a double, a String or a char, and it is one name over many methods.
frames.ask:
If they all have the same name, how can the compiler possibly know
which you meant?

frames.teach:
Specifically, from their number, their types and their order. That combination, together with the name, is called the method signature, and it is the thing that must be unique.

public class Area {    public static double area(double side) {        return side * side;    }    public static double area(double width, double height) {        return width * height;    }    public static int area(int side) {        return side * side;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println(area(3.0));        System.out.println(area(3.0, 4.0));        System.out.println(area(3));    }}
Output9.0
12.0
9

Three methods called area.
frames.ask: Which of the three did area(3) reach, and how do you know?

frames.check: The int one, because it printed 9 and not 9.0.
frames.teach: The argument was an int literal, so the int signature matched exactly. That is the whole mechanism, and it happens at compile time, which is the word the question asks for: overloading is resolved statically, by the compiler, before anything runs.
frames.ask: Now the crucial question. Is the RETURN TYPE part of the signature?

frames.check: No, and this is the mark.
frames.teach: The signature is the method name plus the parameter list: number, types and order. The return type is not part of it. So two methods differing only in return type will not compile: the compiler could never tell them apart, because a call does not have to use the value.
frames.ask: Would int f(int a) and double f(int a) compile?

frames.teach:
Same name, same parameter list, so same
signature, so a duplicate. Change a parameter type and it is fine.
frames.ask: Would f(int a, double b) and f(double a, int b) compile together?

frames.teach:
Same types, different order, so the signatures differ. Now the other word in this lesson. static means the method or field belongs to the class itself, not to any one object. 

public class Counter {    static int made = 0;      // one copy, shared by the whole class    int id;                   // one copy per object    Counter() {        made++;        id = made;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Counter a = new Counter();        Counter b = new Counter();        System.out.println("a.id " + a.id + ", b.id " + b.id);        System.out.println("made " + Counter.made);    }}
frames.ask: Read this and say why made reaches 2 while each id differs.

frames.check:
Because static is one shared copy and instance is one
copy per object.
frames.teach:
Outputa.id 1, b.id 2
made 2

made is static, so both objects increment the same counter. id is an instance field, so each object has its own.
frames.ask: How do you call a static method, and how an instance one?

frames.check:
Static through the class name, instance through an
object.
frames.teach: Counter.made and Math.sqrt(9); against a.id and account.deposit(500). And the rule that trips people: a static method cannot use instance fields directly, because it may run when no object exists. That is the error message "non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context", and it is the commonest compile error in a first Java exam.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The two mark answer, word for word
blocks.html:
Define method overloading, and state the role of the signature.

Method overloading is defining more than one method with the same name in the same class, where the methods differ in their parameter lists. It lets one name serve several related operations on different kinds or numbers of input.

The method signature is the method's name together with the number, types and order of its parameters. It does not include the return type. Because every overloaded method must have a distinct signature, the compiler can match the number, types and order of the arguments at a call site against exactly one of them and bind the call to that method at compile time. This is why overloading is described as static, or compile time, polymorphism.

staticinstance
Belongs tothe classone object
Copiesexactly one, sharedone per object
Called throughthe class name, Math.sqrt(9)an object, acct.deposit(50)
May useonly static members directlyboth static and instance members

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Saying the return type distinguishes overloads. It does not, and this is exactly what the word "precisely" in the question is testing.
  • Confusing overloading with overriding. Overloading is same name, different parameters, same class, resolved by the compiler. Overriding is same name AND same parameters, in a subclass, resolved at run time. Lesson 3.4 does that one.
  • Calling an instance method from main without an object. main is static, so it needs new first.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. What exactly is a method signature?

2. Is the return type part of it?

3. Do void f(int a, double b) and void f(double a, int b) overload legally?

4. Why can a static method not use an instance field directly?
blocks.answer: 1. The method name plus the number, types and order of its parameters. 2. No. 3. Yes, the order differs so the signatures differ. 4. Because it belongs to the class and may run when no object exists, so there is no instance whose field it could mean.

blocks.big:
Signature is name plus parameter list. Never the return type. That is what
lets the compiler pick, at compile time.
blocks.sub: static belongs to the class, instance belongs to an object. One shared copy against one copy each.

title: Arrays, and the Four Patterns the Exam Wants
lead:
Question Three of the last paper was an array walk worth 25 marks, and it
asked for the work to be done in methods that return. These four patterns answer that
question, the mock version of it, and most of Section A besides.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Declare, fill and walk an array; write the four exam patterns as methods that return a value (total, largest, count matching, and find the first index); walk a one pass comparison of neighbours; and index a two dimensional array.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: An array is a fixed row of boxes, all of the same type, numbered from 0. You declare it with square brackets after the type and you can fill it on the spot with braces: int[] scores = {60, 55, 65, 80};.
frames.ask: That array has four values. What is the index of the last one?

frames.teach:
That off-by-one is the single most common array error. Its size is scores.length, and the last index is always length - 1.

public class Arr {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] scores = {60, 55, 65, 80};        System.out.println(scores[0]);        System.out.println(scores[scores.length - 1]);        System.out.println(scores.length);        scores[1] = 99;        System.out.println(scores[1]);    }}
Output60
80
4
99
frames.ask: Notice length has no brackets. What is length on a String?

frames.teach: An array's length is a field; a String's length() is a method. Getting them the wrong way round will not compile, and the examiner plants it.
frames.ask: Now the walk. Write the for loop header that visits every element of a.

frames.teach: Learn it as one thing: zero, less than length, plus plus. Not <=, which runs off the end and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. That header is the opening line of every one of the four patterns.
frames.ask:
Before you look, sketch a method that totals an int array and returns the
total.

frames.check:
Here are all four, as the exam wants them: as methods
that RETURN.
frames.teach:
public class Patterns {    public static int total(int[] a) {        int sum = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {            sum += a[i];        }        return sum;    }    public static int largest(int[] a) {        int max = a[0];        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {            if (a[i] > max) {                max = a[i];            }        }        return max;    }    public static int countAbove(int[] a, int mark) {        int n = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {            if (a[i] > mark) {                n++;            }        }        return n;    }    public static int firstIndexOf(int[] a, int wanted) {        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {            if (a[i] == wanted) {                return i;            }        }        return -1;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] s = {60, 55, 65, 80, 45};        System.out.println("total    " + total(s));        System.out.println("largest  " + largest(s));        System.out.println("above 50 " + countAbove(s, 50));        System.out.println("index of 65 " + firstIndexOf(s, 65));        System.out.println("index of 99 " + firstIndexOf(s, 99));    }}
Outputtotal    305
largest  80
above 50 4
index of 65 2
index of 99 -1
frames.ask: Look at largest. Why does it start at a[0] and loop from 1, rather than starting at 0?

frames.check:
Because the first element is the only safe starting
guess.
frames.teach: Starting max = 0 is wrong the moment every value is negative, which is exactly the case an examiner picks. Start with a[0], then compare from index 1.
frames.ask: And why does firstIndexOf return −1 at the end?

frames.teach:
because every real index is
0 or more. That convention is standard, and returning from inside the loop the moment you find
it is deliberate: it stops looking, which is what "first" means.
Now the paper's own question. It defines a consecutive duplicate as any position i, with i at least 1, where a[i] == a[i-1], and asks for one pass that returns the count.
frames.ask:
Why must that loop start at i = 1 rather than
0?

frames.teach:
Position 0 has nothing before it to compare with, so the comparison only makes sense from 1 onwards. The paper says so in its own definition, and the loop must match it.

public class Duplicates {    public static int countConsecutive(int[] a) {        int n = 0;        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) {            if (a[i] == a[i - 1]) {                n++;            }        }        return n;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] sales = {20, 20, 35, 40, 40, 40, 15, 60, 60, 25};        System.out.println(countConsecutive(sales));    }}
Output4

The array is 20, 20, 35, 40, 40, 40, 15, 60, 60, 25 and the answer is 4.
frames.ask: Check it by hand: which four positions matched?

frames.teach: Note that the run of three 40s gives two matches, not one: positions 4 and 5 each equal the one before them. That is the detail the question is really testing, and the paper's hint, that it must not flag 35, 15 or 25, is a free check on your answer.
frames.ask: Now two dimensions. What does marks[2][1] mean?

frames.teach:
A two dimensional array is an array of arrays: the first index picks the row, the second picks within it.

public class Table2D {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[][] marks = {{60, 70}, {55, 65}, {80, 90}};        System.out.println(marks.length);        System.out.println(marks[0].length);        System.out.println(marks[2][1]);        for (int r = 0; r < marks.length; r++) {            for (int c = 0; c < marks[r].length; c++) {                System.out.print(marks[r][c] + " ");            }            System.out.println();        }    }}
Output3
2
90
60 70 
55 65 
80 90

marks.length is the number of rows; marks[r].length is the width of row r.
frames.ask:
Why ask each row for its own length rather than using one number
for all of them?

frames.check: Because rows need not be the same length.
frames.teach:
Java
allows ragged arrays, and asking each row for its own length is the habit that works either
way. Two nested loops, outer over rows, inner over columns, and that is every table question
answered.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The four patterns, as method headers
blocks.html:
PatternHeaderInside
Totalstatic int total(int[] a)sum = 0 before, sum += a[i] inside, return sum after
Largeststatic int largest(int[] a)max = a[0], loop from 1, if (a[i] > max) max = a[i]
Count matchingstatic int countAbove(int[] a, int mark)n = 0, if (test) n++, return n
Find firststatic int firstIndexOf(int[] a, int x)if (a[i] == x) return i; inside the loop, return -1; after it

The walk, learned as one thing: for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++). Zero, less than length, plus plus.

And the neighbour walk: for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) comparing a[i] with a[i-1]. Start at 1, because index 0 has no neighbour behind it.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• i <= a.length. One step too far, and an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time.
  • a.length() on an array, or s.length on a String. Arrays have a field, Strings have a method.
  • Starting max = 0. Wrong for an array of negatives. Start at a[0].
  • An int[] filled with decimals. {24.0, 40.0} in an int array does not compile, and it is on the last paper.
  • Printing instead of returning when the question says the method returns the count.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. For int[] a = {5, 3, 9};, what are a.length and the last valid index?

2. Write the method header for one that returns the average of an int array.

3. Why must the neighbour comparison loop start at 1?

4. On paper, write largest from memory, then check the starting value.
blocks.answer: 1. 3 and 2. 2. public static double average(int[] a), double because the answer may not be whole, and remember the cast inside. 3. Because index 0 has no element before it and a[-1] would throw. 4. int max = a[0]; then loop from 1.

blocks.big:
Zero, less than length, plus plus. Total, largest, count, find. Four patterns,
each a method that returns.
blocks.sub: Largest starts at a[0], not 0. Neighbours start at 1, not 0. Those two starting points are where the marks are lost.

title: Strings, and Why == Destroys Programs
lead: Every question that reads a name, a tier or a command compares text, and Section B of the 2024/2025 paper needed a string built inside a loop. Get == wrong and the program compiles, runs, and silently answers no to everything.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Use the string methods by name; explain with a listing why comparing text with == is wrong and equals is right; say what immutable means and what follows from it; and build a string in a loop with StringBuilder.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A String is not a primitive. It is an object, and a String variable holds a reference to it: an arrow pointing at the text, not the text itself.
frames.ask: Given that, what do you think == compares when you put it between two Strings?

frames.teach:
It asks "are these the same object?", not "do these say the same thing?". Sometimes the answer accidentally comes out right, which is what makes it dangerous.

public class Compare {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String a = "gold";        String b = "gold";        String c = new String("gold");        System.out.println(a == b);        System.out.println(a == c);        System.out.println(a.equals(c));        System.out.println(a.equalsIgnoreCase("GOLD"));    }}
Outputtrue
false
true
true
frames.ask: Look at the first two lines. a == b was true but a == c was false, and all three say "gold". Why?

frames.check: Because a and b are literals, and Java shares one copy of each identical literal.
frames.teach: They ended up pointing at the same object by luck. new String("gold") forces a separate object, so the arrows differ and == says false even though the text is identical.
frames.ask: And what did a.equals(c) say?

frames.teach: because equals compares the characters. That is the rule, and it has no exceptions worth knowing: always compare text with equals, never with ==. Use equalsIgnoreCase when case should not matter, which is usually what you want for a typed answer.
frames.ask:
Why is this so much more dangerous than a normal
bug?

frames.teach: Nothing warns you. It works in your small test, where literals are shared, and fails the moment the text comes from Scanner or a dialog, because that text is a new object every time. A whole question can score zero from one ==.
Now the methods. There are eight worth knowing, and every one of them returns a new String and leaves the original untouched.
frames.ask: Given that, what does s.toUpperCase(); on its own line achieve?

frames.teach:
It builds an upper case copy and throws it away. You must assign it: s = s.toUpperCase();. Here are the eight, all at once.

public class StrMethods {    public static void main(String[] args) {        String s = "  Serve Jesus Now  ";        System.out.println("[" + s.trim() + "]");        System.out.println(s.trim().length());        System.out.println(s.toUpperCase().trim());        System.out.println(s.trim().charAt(0));        System.out.println(s.trim().substring(6));        System.out.println(s.trim().substring(0, 5));        System.out.println(s.indexOf("Jesus"));        System.out.println(s.trim().replace("Now", "Today"));    }}
Output[Serve Jesus Now]
15
SERVE JESUS NOW
S
Jesus Now
Serve
8
Serve Jesus Today
frames.ask: Look at substring(0, 5), which gave "Serve". Is the second number included?

frames.teach: substring(start, end) takes from start up to but not including end, so the length is end - start. With one argument it runs to the end of the string. That off-by-one is worth checking twice in an exam.
frames.ask: Why is it called immutable, and what are the two consequences?

frames.check: Because once made, its characters can never change.
frames.teach: Two consequences, and they are the marks: every method returns a new String, so you must assign the result; and because the contents are fixed a String is safe to share and can be used as a key in a lookup.
frames.ask: If Strings cannot change, what happens when you build one up inside a loop with s = s + x;?

frames.check: A brand new String is created on every pass,
frames.teach:
and the old one is thrown away. For a handful of items that is fine and the examiner accepts it. For many it is wasteful, and Java gives you a mutable alternative.

public class Build {    public static void main(String[] args) {        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();        int[] a = {20, 20, 35, 40};        for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {            if (i > 0) {                sb.append(", ");            }            sb.append(a[i]);        }        System.out.println(sb.toString());    }}
Output20, 20, 35, 40

StringBuilder can be changed in place: append adds to it and toString() hands you the finished String.
frames.ask:
One warning. The 2025/2026 paper's Question Three says to build its list
"using plain String concatenation only, no StringBuilder". So which do you use there?

frames.check: Plain concatenation, because the paper said so.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The eight methods, and the one rule
blocks.html:
MethodDoesExample on "Serve Jesus Now"
length()how many characters15
charAt(i)the character at index i, from 0charAt(0) is 'S'
substring(a, b)from a up to but NOT including bsubstring(0,5) is "Serve"
indexOf(x)where x starts, or −1 if absentindexOf("Jesus") is 6
equals(x)same characters, true or falsethe ONLY way to compare text
equalsIgnoreCase(x)the same, ignoring casefor anything the user typed
toUpperCase(), toLowerCase()a converted copyassign it or it is lost
trim()a copy with the ends strippedalways trim typed input
replace(a, b)a copy with every a swappedassign it or it is lost

The one rule: a String is immutable. Every method above returns a new String and changes nothing. If you did not assign the result, nothing happened.

And the one that decides questions: == compares references, equals compares characters. Always equals for text.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Why can a == b be true for two Strings that say the same thing, and false for two others that also do?

2. After s = "cat"; s.toUpperCase(); what is in s?

3. What is "PROGRAM".substring(2, 5)?

4. Write the test for a tier typed by the user being Gold, however they capitalised it.
blocks.answer: 1. == compares references; identical literals share one object, but a String built at run time is a different object. 2. Still "cat"; the result was never assigned. 3. "OGR": from index 2 up to but not including 5. 4. if (tier.trim().equalsIgnoreCase("Gold")).

blocks.big:
equals compares the text, == compares the arrows. Every string method hands
you a new string and leaves the old one alone.
blocks.sub: If a string operation seems to have done nothing, you forgot to assign it. And if a text comparison seems always false, you used ==.
