title: Classes, Objects and Constructors
lead:
Question Four of the last paper was a bank account hierarchy worth 25 marks,
and its first nine marks were exactly this: a class with private fields and a constructor
that initialises all three. Everything else on Day 3 is built on this page.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Define a class with fields and methods, create objects from it, define a class, an object, an attribute and a method in the examiner's terms, and write a constructor that initialises every field.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A class is a blueprint. It says what every thing of that kind will know and what it will be able to do. An object is one actual thing built from that blueprint.
frames.ask:
Using a house as the analogy, which is the architect's drawing
and which is the building?

frames.check:
The class is the drawing, the object is the
building.
frames.teach:
One drawing, many buildings, each with its own address and its own paint. The things it knows are attributes, also called fields or instance variables. The things it can do are methods. 

class Student {    String name;    int score;    void show() {        System.out.println(name + " scored " + score);    }}public class UseStudent {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Student a = new Student();        a.name = "Ada";        a.score = 72;        a.show();        Student b = new Student();        b.name = "Victor";        b.score = 65;        b.show();    }}
frames.ask:
Read this and say how many objects
exist.

frames.teach:
a and b.

OutputAda scored 72
Victor scored 65

Each has its own name and its own score: that is what "one copy per object" means.
frames.ask:
Which word actually built each
object?

frames.teach: new Student() allocates a fresh object and hands you a reference to it, which you keep in a variable. Then the dot reaches inside: a.name is that object's name, a.show() is that object's method.
frames.ask: What is in a field you never set?

frames.check: A default, not a random value.
frames.teach:
class Empty {    String name;    int score;    boolean passed;}public class Defaults {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Empty e = new Empty();        System.out.println(e.name);        System.out.println(e.score);        System.out.println(e.passed);    }}
Outputnull
0
false

Numbers start at 0, booleans at false, and any object reference, including a String, at null.
frames.ask: Why is that null dangerous?

frames.check: Because calling a method on it crashes.
frames.teach: e.name.length() throws a NullPointerException: there is no object there to ask. That is the argument for setting every field as the object is born, which is what the next stage is about.

Setting each field by hand after new is four lines of opportunity to forget one. A constructor does it at the moment of creation, and it is what the paper means by "provide a constructor to initialise all three".
frames.ask:
A constructor has two rules that no other method has. Guess
them.

frames.check:
It has the same name as the class, and it has no return
type at all.
frames.teach:
Not even void. Those two together are how Java recognises it.

class Student {    String name;    int score;    Student(String name, int score) {        this.name = name;        this.score = score;    }    void show() {        System.out.println(name + " scored " + score);    }}public class UseCtor {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Student a = new Student("Ada", 72);        Student b = new Student("Victor", 65);        a.show();        b.show();    }}
OutputAda scored 72
Victor scored 65

Same output as before, but the object cannot exist half built.
frames.ask: Look at this.name = name;. Why is this needed?

frames.check:
Because the parameter and the field have the same
name.
frames.teach: this.name means the field belonging to this object, and plain name means the parameter. Without this, the line assigns the parameter to itself and the field stays null: a silent, complete failure that compiles.
frames.ask: Could you avoid this by naming the parameter something else?

frames.teach: Matching names read better and the examiner expects this; it is standard Java and it shows you know what it means.
frames.ask: If you write no constructor at all, can you still say new Student()?

frames.check:
Yes: Java supplies a default one, taking no
arguments.
frames.teach: But the moment you write any constructor of your own, that free one disappears. So if you write Student(String, int) and then call new Student(), it will not compile. Write both if you need both: constructors can be overloaded like any other method, by parameter list.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The four definitions, and the class shape
blocks.html:
WordThe definition to write
Classa blueprint or template that defines the attributes and methods common to all objects of that kind
Objectan instance of a class, created with new, with its own copy of the attributes
Attributea variable declared in the class that holds part of an object's state; also called a field or instance variable
Methoda named block of code inside a class that defines a behaviour an object can perform
Constructora special method with the same name as the class and no return type, run automatically by new to initialise a new object
class Student {    private String name;              // attributes: one copy per object    private int score;    Student(String name, int score) {   // constructor: same name, NO return type        this.name = name;              // this.field = parameter        this.score = score;    }    void show() { ... }                // methods: behaviour}

Defaults for fields never set: numbers 0, boolean false, every object reference null.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Giving the constructor a return type. void Student(...) is not a constructor, it is an ordinary method that happens to share the name, and new Student(...) will not find it.
  • Forgetting this. name = name; assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field null.
  • Calling new Student() after writing your own constructor. The free default one is gone.
  • Putting the class inside main. Classes sit beside each other in the file, not inside another method.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Define a class and an object in one sentence each.

2. What two things make a constructor different from every other method?

3. What is in an unset String field, and what happens if you call a method on it?

4. On paper, write a class Book with a title, a price and a constructor that sets both.
blocks.answer: 1. A class is a blueprint defining the attributes and methods of a kind of thing; an object is one instance of it, made with new. 2. Same name as the class, and no return type at all. 3. null, and calling a method on it throws NullPointerException. 4. class Book { private String title; private double price; Book(String title, double price) { this.title = title; this.price = price; } }

blocks.big:
Class is the blueprint, object is the building, new is the builder. A
constructor shares the class name and has no return type.
blocks.sub: this.field = parameter, on every line of every constructor. Leave out this and the field stays empty, silently.

title: Encapsulation: Private Fields, Public Doors
lead:
Question Two of the last paper opened with "Define encapsulation as an OOP
principle", for two marks, and Question Four then asked you to build a class using it. The
definition and the implementation are both examined, so learn both.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Define encapsulation as an object oriented principle in two sentences, and implement it: private fields, public getters and setters, and a setter that refuses a value that would break the object.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: In Lesson 3.1 the fields were open: anything could write a.score = -500; and the object had no say.
frames.ask:
What is wrong with
that, in one word?

frames.check: Control, or the lack of it.
frames.teach: An object should be responsible for its own state, and it cannot be if anybody can reach in and change it. So encapsulation does two things together: it makes the data private, and it provides public methods as the only way in.
frames.ask:
If the fields are private, how does anything outside read the
balance?

frames.check: Through a public method that returns it.
frames.teach:
That is a getter, named getBalance() by convention. The one that changes a value is a setter, named setBalance(double b). Together they are the doors.

class Account {    private String holder;    private double balance;    Account(String holder, double balance) {        this.holder = holder;        this.balance = balance;    }    public String getHolder() {        return holder;    }    public double getBalance() {        return balance;    }    public void deposit(double amount) {        if (amount > 0) {            balance += amount;        } else {            System.out.println("Deposit must be positive");        }    }}public class UseAccount {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Account a = new Account("Ada", 500);        a.deposit(250);        a.deposit(-40);        System.out.println(a.getHolder() + " has " + a.getBalance());    }}
OutputDeposit must be positive
Ada has 750.0
frames.ask: Look at what deposit(-40) did. Why is that the whole point?

frames.teach: The method checked first. With a public field there is nowhere to put that check, so nothing can stop a negative deposit. Encapsulation is what makes validation possible, and that sentence is worth saying in your answer.
frames.ask:
Name the four access modifiers, from most open to
most closed.

frames.teach: public is reachable from anywhere; private only from inside its own class; protected from inside the class and from subclasses; and writing nothing at all gives package access, reachable from other classes in the same folder.
frames.ask:
Which one do fields normally get, and
which do methods?

frames.teach: That is the rule of thumb the examiner is looking for: private data, public behaviour. And protected earns its place in the next lesson, where a subclass needs to reach a parent's field.
frames.ask:
Last one. Say what encapsulation buys you, in three
words.

frames.teach:
Control,
because only the class's own methods touch its data. Validation, because those methods can
refuse bad values. Safe change, because you can rewrite how the data is stored without
breaking anybody, so long as the public methods keep their shape. Those three are the
"advantages" half of the question.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
The two mark answer, word for word. Encapsulation is the object oriented principle of binding an object's data and the methods that operate on that data together in a single unit, the class, while hiding the internal state from outside access. It is achieved in Java by declaring the fields private and providing public methods, typically getters and setters, as the only route to them. Its benefits are control, because the class alone can change its own state; validation, because a setter can reject an invalid value; and maintainability, because the internal representation can be changed without affecting any code that uses the class.

class Account {    private double balance;                // 1. data is PRIVATE    public double getBalance() {            // 2. a getter to read        return balance;    }    public void deposit(double amount) {     // 3. a method to change,        if (amount > 0) {                    //    which VALIDATES first            balance += amount;        }    }}
ModifierReachable from
publicanywhere
protectedthe class, its subclasses, and the same package
(nothing)the same package only
privatethe class itself only

The four pillars, since the paper compares them: encapsulation hides data behind methods; abstraction shows what a thing does and hides how; inheritance lets one class take another's members; polymorphism lets one call behave differently depending on the object. Lessons 3.3 and 3.4 do the last two.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Writing getters and setters but leaving the fields public. That is not encapsulation, it is decoration. The private is the point.
  • A setter with no check in it. If it simply assigns whatever it is given, it has bought you nothing over a public field. Put the validation in.
  • Confusing encapsulation with abstraction. Encapsulation hides the DATA; abstraction hides the IMPLEMENTATION. Say both if asked to distinguish them.
  • Reaching a private field from main. It will not compile. Go through the getter.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Define encapsulation in two sentences.

2. Name the four access modifiers, most open first.

3. What can a private field plus a setter do that a public field cannot?

4. On paper, write a Student class with a private score, a getter, and a setter that rejects anything outside 0 to 100.
blocks.answer: 1. See the memorise box. 2. public, protected, default, private. 3. Refuse an invalid value, because the assignment goes through code that can check it first. 4. private int score; public int getScore() returns it; public void setScore(int s) with if (s >= 0 && s <= 100) score = s; else a message.

blocks.big:
Private data, public doors. The doors are what let the object refuse a value
that would break it.
blocks.sub: Encapsulation hides the data, abstraction hides the how. Two different pillars, two different answers.

title: Inheritance
lead: Question Four of the last paper: a superclass BankAccount with private fields and a constructor, then subclasses that add their own behaviour. Nine marks for the parent, the rest for the children. This lesson is that question.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write a subclass that extends a superclass, call the parent constructor with super, say what is inherited and what is not, and build the two level hierarchy Section B of the paper asks for.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A savings account is a bank account, and so is a current account. They share a number, a holder and a balance, and they share depositing and withdrawing. Writing all of that twice would be duplication. Inheritance lets one class take another's members and add to them.
frames.ask:
Which keyword do you think says "takes
from"?

frames.teach:
class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount means: everything BankAccount has, SavingsAccount has too, plus whatever it adds. The one being extended is the superclass or parent; the one extending is the subclass or child. 

class BankAccount {    private String number;    private String holder;    protected double balance;    BankAccount(String number, String holder, double balance) {        this.number = number;        this.holder = holder;        this.balance = balance;    }    public void deposit(double amount) {        balance += amount;    }    public void withdraw(double amount) {        if (amount <= balance) {            balance -= amount;        } else {            System.out.println("REJECTED: insufficient funds");        }    }    public void display() {        System.out.println(number + " " + holder + " " + balance);    }}class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {    private double rate;    SavingsAccount(String n, String h, double b, double rate) {        super(n, h, b);        this.rate = rate;    }    public void addInterest() {        balance += balance * rate;    }}public class UseBank {    public static void main(String[] args) {        SavingsAccount s = new SavingsAccount("101", "Ada", 1000, 0.05);        s.deposit(500);        s.addInterest();        s.display();        s.withdraw(50000);    }}
frames.ask:
Read this and find the one line that connects the child's constructor to
the parent's.

frames.teach:
Output101 Ada 1575.0
REJECTED: insufficient funds

super(...) calls the parent's constructor, handing it the three values it needs.
frames.ask: Where must that line sit inside the child constructor?

frames.teach:
Java insists,
because the parent's part of the object must exist before the child adds to it. Put anything
above it and it will not compile.
frames.ask: What happens if you leave super(...) out altogether?

frames.check:
Java inserts a silent call to the parent's
no-argument constructor.
frames.teach: Which is fine if there is one, and a compile error if the parent only has a constructor that takes arguments, as ours does. That error, "constructor BankAccount in class BankAccount cannot be applied to given types", means exactly one thing: you forgot super.
frames.ask: Now look at the fields. Why is balance declared protected and not private?

frames.check: So the subclass can touch it.
frames.teach: addInterest needs to change the balance directly. A private field is invisible even to a child, so it would have to go through a public setter instead. protected means: mine, and my children's. That is exactly what it is for, and it is why the paper's hierarchy question is where protected earns its place.
Look again at the main method. s is a SavingsAccount, yet s.deposit(500) and s.display() both work, and neither is written in SavingsAccount.
frames.ask: Where did they come from?

frames.teach:
That is the whole
benefit: the child gets the parent's public and protected members for free, and adds only
what is new.
frames.ask: So what is NOT inherited?

frames.teach: Two things to say if asked. A constructor belongs to its own class and is never inherited, which is why you must call it with super. And a private member exists in the child object but the child's code cannot see it.
frames.ask: How many classes can one class extend in Java?

frames.teach: Java has no multiple inheritance of classes, deliberately, to avoid the ambiguity of inheriting two different versions of the same method. A class may implement as many interfaces as it likes, which is how Java gets the benefit without the ambiguity. That distinction is a favourite objective question.
frames.ask: Can a subclass itself be extended?

frames.check: Yes, as deep as you like.
frames.teach: That is multilevel inheritance: A extends B extends C. And several classes extending the same parent is hierarchical inheritance, which is what the bank question wants: one BankAccount, several kinds of account beside each other.
frames.ask: Name the relationship inheritance expresses, in two words.

frames.teach: A SavingsAccount is a BankAccount. That is the test for whether inheritance is the right tool: if you cannot say "is a" with a straight face, you want a field instead, which is a "has a". A car is not an engine; it has one.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The shape, and the five facts
blocks.html:
class BankAccount {                     // the SUPERCLASS, or parent    private String number;                 // private: mine only    protected double balance;            // protected: mine and my children's    BankAccount(String n, double b) { ... }    public void deposit(double a) { ... }   // inherited by every child}class SavingsAccount extends BankAccount {  // the SUBCLASS, or child    private double rate;                   // what it ADDS    SavingsAccount(String n, double b, double r) {        super(n, b);                       // FIRST statement, always        this.rate = r;    }}
  • extends makes the relationship; super(...) calls the parent's constructor and must be the first statement in the child's.
  • Inherited: public and protected fields and methods. Not inherited: constructors, and anything private.
  • One parent only. Java has no multiple inheritance of classes; use interfaces for that.
  • The kinds: single (one child), multilevel (a chain), hierarchical (several children of one parent). Java supports all three.
  • The test: inheritance is an "is a"; a field is a "has a".

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Forgetting super(...) when the parent has no no-argument constructor. It is a compile error, and it is the commonest one in this question.
  • Putting super(...) after another statement. It must be first.
  • Making a field private and then using it in the child. Use protected, or go through a getter.
  • Redeclaring an inherited field in the child. You then have two, the child's hides the parent's, and half your methods update the wrong one.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Which keyword creates a subclass, and which calls the parent constructor?

2. Name two things that are never inherited.

3. Why is protected used for a field a subclass must change?

4. On paper, write CurrentAccount extends BankAccount with an overdraft limit and a constructor.
blocks.answer: 1. extends, and super(...) as the first statement. 2. Constructors, and private members. 3. Because private is invisible even to a child, while protected means the class and its subclasses. 4. Fields, then a constructor calling super(...) first and setting the limit second.

blocks.big:
extends takes it, super builds it, and super goes first. Public and protected
are inherited; constructors and private are not.
blocks.sub: If you cannot say "a child IS A parent", you want a field, not inheritance. Is a, not has a.

title: Polymorphism, and Overriding against Overloading
lead:
Question Two of the last paper: "State three differences between Method
overloading and Method overriding", three marks. And Question Four asked for a hierarchy
"using inheritance and polymorphism", so the concept is examined twice, once as words and once
as code.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Override a method in a subclass, explain polymorphism with a listing, and state three differences between overloading and overriding.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: A subclass inherits its parent's methods. But sometimes the child needs to do the same job differently: every account can describe itself, and a savings account should describe itself as a savings account. So the child writes its own version of a method the parent already has.
frames.ask: What do you think that is called?

frames.teach:
Same name, same parameters, same return type, in a subclass, replacing the parent's version for objects of that child. 

class Account {    protected double balance;    Account(double balance) {        this.balance = balance;    }    public void describe() {        System.out.println("An account holding " + balance);    }}class Savings extends Account {    Savings(double b) {        super(b);    }    @Override    public void describe() {        System.out.println("A savings account holding " + balance);    }}class Current extends Account {    Current(double b) {        super(b);    }    @Override    public void describe() {        System.out.println("A current account holding " + balance);    }}public class Poly {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Account[] all = {new Savings(1000), new Current(250),                         new Account(10)};        for (int i = 0; i < all.length; i++) {            all[i].describe();        }    }}
frames.ask:
Read this, then predict the three lines it prints. Look carefully at the
array's type.

frames.check: Each object describes itself in its own way.
frames.teach:
OutputA savings account holding 1000.0
A current account holding 250.0
An account holding 10.0

The array is declared Account[], so as far as the compiler knows every element is an Account. Yet the savings object ran the savings version.
frames.ask: What decided which version ran?

frames.check: The actual object, at run time.
frames.teach: Not the declared type. That is polymorphism: one call, all[i].describe(), written once, behaving differently according to what is really there. The word means "many forms", and the mechanism is called dynamic or run time binding.
frames.ask: Why is that useful, rather than merely clever?

frames.check: Because the loop never has to know the kinds.
frames.teach:
Add
a FixedDeposit class tomorrow and that loop does not change by one character. A parent-typed
variable can hold any child, so you can treat a mixed collection uniformly and still get each
one's own behaviour. That sentence is the answer to "why use polymorphism".
frames.ask: What is the @Override line above each method for?

frames.check: It asks the compiler to check.
frames.teach:
If the method does
not actually override anything, because you misspelled the name or got a parameter wrong, it
becomes a compile error instead of a silent new method that never runs. It is optional and
you should always write it.
frames.ask:
Now the comparison. Overloading was Lesson 2.7.
Where does it happen, and where does overriding?

frames.check: Overloading in one class; overriding across two.
frames.teach: And that is the first of the three differences the paper wants. The second is the parameters: overloading must change them, overriding must keep them identical. The third is when it is decided: overloading at compile time by the signature, overriding at run time by the object.
frames.ask:
Say all three back before you read the
table.

frames.teach: Learn them in that order and you can always produce three. There is a fourth if you need it: an overridden method may not be less accessible than the one it replaces, so a public method cannot be overridden as private.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.html:
OverloadingOverriding
Wherewithin the SAME classacross TWO classes, a subclass replacing its superclass's version
ParametersMUST differ, in number, type or orderMUST be identical, and so must the return type
Decidedat COMPILE time, from the signature. Static bindingat RUN time, from the actual object. Dynamic binding
Also calledcompile time polymorphismrun time polymorphism
Accessanythingmay not be made more restrictive than the parent's

The definition of polymorphism to write: polymorphism is the object oriented principle by which a single method call can produce different behaviour depending on the actual type of the object it is called on. In Java it is achieved by overriding a superclass method in a subclass and then referring to the object through a superclass reference, so that the version executed is chosen at run time by the object rather than at compile time by the declared type.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Changing the parameters while meaning to override. Different parameters means you have OVERLOADED it, not overridden it, and the parent's version still runs. This is exactly what @Override catches.
  • Saying overriding happens at compile time. It is the run time one. Getting the two timings the wrong way round loses the mark that "at compile time" in the overloading question was testing.
  • Forgetting that static methods are not overridden. They are hidden, and the declared type decides. Do not use a static method as your polymorphism example.
  • Writing three differences that are really one. Class, parameters, timing are three independent facts; "different class" and "in a subclass" are the same fact twice.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. State three differences between overloading and overriding.

2. An Account variable holds a Savings object. Whose describe() runs, and when is that decided?

3. What does @Override do for you?

4. Define polymorphism in one sentence.
blocks.answer: 1. Same class against subclass; parameters must differ against must match; decided at compile time against run time. 2. Savings, decided at run time from the actual object. 3. Makes the compiler check that a method really does override something, so a typo becomes an error instead of a silent new method. 4. One call producing different behaviour according to the actual type of the object it is made on.

blocks.big:
Overloading: same class, different parameters, compile time. Overriding:
subclass, identical parameters, run time.
blocks.sub: Class, parameters, timing. Three words that give you the three marks every year.

blocks.label: Now prove it
blocks.tag: every objective question on this topic

title: Recursion
lead:
Recursion has its own objective questions, and factorial is the one every
paper reaches for. Two rules and one trace, and you own the topic.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write the standard recursions, name the base case and the recursive case in any recursive method, trace one by hand, and say when recursion is worse than a loop.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Recursion is a method that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem. Factorial is the classic: 5! is 5 times 4!, and 4! is 4 times 3!, and so on.
frames.ask: If every call makes another call, what stops it?

frames.check: A case that does not call again.
frames.teach:
That is the base case, and every recursive method must have one. The part that does call again is the recursive case. Two parts, always.

public class Fact {    public static int factorial(int n) {        if (n <= 1) {            return 1;        }        return n * factorial(n - 1);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println(factorial(5));        for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {            System.out.print(factorial(i) + " ");        }        System.out.println();    }}
Output120
1 2 6 24 120
frames.ask: Point at the base case and the recursive case in that method.

frames.teach: Note what makes it terminate: each call is on a smaller n, so the base case is always approached.
frames.ask: What would happen if the recursive call were factorial(n)?

frames.check: It would never reach the base case.
frames.teach: Every call would make an identical call, the call stack would fill, and the program would die with StackOverflowError. That is the recursive equivalent of an infinite loop, and it is the error to name if asked what goes wrong without a base case.
frames.ask: Now trace factorial(4). Write the four calls going down, then the values coming back up.

frames.teach:
Going downWaiting forComing back up
factorial(4)4 × factorial(3)4 × 6 = 24
factorial(3)3 × factorial(2)3 × 2 = 6
factorial(2)2 × factorial(1)2 × 1 = 2
factorial(1)nothing, it is the base case1

Nothing multiplies until the bottom is reached. That is the shape of every recursion trace, and drawing it as two columns is how you answer a "what does this return" question. 

public class Recs {    public static int sumTo(int n) {        if (n == 0) {            return 0;        }        return n + sumTo(n - 1);    }    public static int fib(int n) {        if (n <= 1) {            return n;        }        return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);    }    public static String reverse(String s) {        if (s.length() <= 1) {            return s;        }        return reverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println(sumTo(5));        System.out.println(fib(7));        System.out.println(reverse("JAVA"));    }}
frames.ask: Here are three more standards. Predict all three outputs.

frames.teach:
Output15
13
AVAJ

Sum to 5 is 15; the seventh Fibonacci number counting from 0 is 13; and reversing "JAVA" gives "AVAJ". Look at reverse: it puts the first character on the end of the reversed rest, which is the whole trick.
frames.ask: Now the comparison. Which uses more memory, recursion or a loop?

frames.teach: Every call in progress occupies a frame on the call stack, holding its own copy of the parameters, and none is released until the base case returns. A loop uses one set of variables however many times it goes round. So recursion is clearer for problems that are naturally self similar, and heavier in memory and usually slower.
frames.ask:
Which would you use to total an array in an
exam?

frames.check: A loop, unless the question says recursion.
frames.teach: Iteration is the right default; recursion is right when the problem defines itself in terms of itself, or when the paper asks for it by name. fib above is the honest warning: it recalculates the same values over and over, and by n = 40 it is unusably slow.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The two rules and the four standards
blocks.html:
Every recursive method has exactly two parts, and an answer that names them is halfway to the marks:

  1. a base case, a condition under which it returns without calling itself;
  2. a recursive case, which calls itself on a smaller input, so that the base case is always approached.
StandardBase caseRecursive case
Factorialn <= 1 returns 1n * factorial(n - 1)
Sum to nn == 0 returns 0n + sumTo(n - 1)
Fibonaccin <= 1 returns nfib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
Reverse a Stringlength 1 or less returns itreverse(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0)

Recursion against iteration, the comparison answer: recursion expresses a self similar problem more clearly and in fewer lines, but each call occupies a stack frame, so it uses more memory and is generally slower, and without a correct base case it ends in StackOverflowError. Iteration uses one set of variables and constant memory, and is preferred unless the problem is naturally recursive.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Name the two parts every recursive method must have.

2. Trace factorial(4) and give the value returned at each level.

3. What error results from a missing or unreachable base case?

4. Write, on paper, a recursive method that counts down from n printing each number.
blocks.answer: 1. A base case that returns without recursing, and a recursive case that calls itself on a smaller input. 2. 1, 2, 6, 24. 3. StackOverflowError. 4. static void down(int n) { if (n < 1) return; System.out.println(n); down(n - 1); }

blocks.big:
Base case stops it, recursive case shrinks it. Nothing is computed on the way
down; everything is computed on the way back up.
blocks.sub: Draw the trace as two columns, down and up. That drawing answers every "what does this return" question on recursion.

blocks.label: Now prove it
blocks.tag: every objective question on this topic

title: Exceptions: Checked, Unchecked, try catch finally
lead: Question One part B of the last paper: "State three differences between checked exceptions and unchecked exceptions in Java", three marks. And Question Five needed throw new IllegalArgumentException. Both are on this page.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: State three differences between checked and unchecked exceptions; name the common exceptions and what causes each; wrap risky work in try, catch and finally; and throw an exception deliberately when a value is invalid.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: An exception is a fault that happens while the program is running, in code that compiled perfectly, because the situation turned out to be impossible.
frames.ask: How is that different from a syntax error?

frames.check:
A syntax error is caught by the compiler, so nothing
runs at all.
frames.teach:
An exception happens mid-run, and if nothing handles it the program stops there and prints a stack trace. 

public class Kinds {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try {            int n = Integer.parseInt("abc");        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {            System.out.println("NumberFormatException caught");        }        try {            int[] a = {1, 2, 3};            System.out.println(a[5]);        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {            System.out.println("ArrayIndexOutOfBounds caught");        }        try {            System.out.println(10 / 0);        } catch (ArithmeticException e) {            System.out.println("ArithmeticException: " + e.getMessage());        }        String s = null;        try {            System.out.println(s.length());        } catch (NullPointerException e) {            System.out.println("NullPointerException caught");        }    }}
frames.ask:
Read these four and name the exception each
one will raise before you look.

frames.teach:
OutputNumberFormatException caught
ArrayIndexOutOfBounds caught
ArithmeticException: / by zero
NullPointerException caught

Those four cover most of what an exam program can do wrong. The shape is try { risky } then catch (TypeOfProblem e) { what to do }.
frames.ask: If the try block succeeds, does the catch block run?

frames.teach: A catch runs only when its exception actually occurs. And the variable e holds the exception object, so e.getMessage() gives the detail, which is why the division line could print "/ by zero".
frames.ask:
Now the distinction the paper asks about. Which of those four
did Java force you to handle?

frames.teach: All four are unchecked: the compiler does not insist you deal with them, because they are programming faults you should prevent rather than catch. Checked exceptions are the other kind, and the compiler will not let you ignore them.
frames.ask:
Which everyday operation do you think
raises a checked exception?

frames.teach: The file might not be there, and that is not your bug, it is the world being uncooperative. So IOException and FileNotFoundException are checked, and Java makes you either catch them or declare throws on your method, which is why Lesson 3.7's listings say throws IOException.

There is a third block. finally runs every time, whether the try succeeded, failed, or returned in the middle. 

public class Finally {    public static int read(String text) {        try {            int n = Integer.parseInt(text);            System.out.println("parsed " + n);            return n;        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {            System.out.println("not a number: " + text);            return -1;        } finally {            System.out.println("  (finally always runs)");        }    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        read("72");        read("seventy");    }}
frames.ask: Predict all six lines this prints.

frames.teach:
Outputparsed 72
  (finally always runs)
not a number: seventy
  (finally always runs)

Look at the first call: it returned from inside the try, and the finally still ran before the method actually left.
frames.ask:
What is finally FOR, in one
word?

frames.teach:
Closing a file, closing a connection:
anything that must happen whatever went wrong. That is the answer to "what is the purpose of
finally".
frames.ask:
Now the other direction. How do you raise an exception
deliberately?

frames.teach: The paper's ticket question needs exactly that: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Day must be 1, 2 or 3"); in the default of its switch. Note the two words: throw raises one now, throws in a method header warns that this method might.
frames.ask: One letter apart. Which goes in the header?

frames.teach: public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException says: I am not handling this, my caller must. That is the lazy but perfectly legal way to satisfy the compiler for a checked exception, and it is what the file listings use so the code stays short.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The three mark answer, and the shape
blocks.html:
CheckedUnchecked
Checked by the compilerYES: you must catch it or declare throws, or the program will not compileNO: the compiler says nothing
When knownat compile timeonly at run time
Inherits fromException, but not RuntimeExceptionRuntimeException
Caused byconditions outside the program: a missing file, a broken connectionfaults in the program's own logic: a bad index, a null, a divide by zero
ExamplesIOException, FileNotFoundException, SQLExceptionNullPointerException, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, NumberFormatException
try {    // the risky work, and only the risky work} catch (NumberFormatException e) {    // what to do about THAT problem. e.getMessage() has the detail} finally {    // cleanup: runs every time, success or failure or return}

The two words: throw new X(...) raises one now; throws X in a header declares that this method may raise one and is not handling it.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Catching Exception for everything. It hides real bugs including your own typing mistakes. Name the exception you expect.
  • Wrapping the whole program in one try. Then you cannot tell which line failed. Wrap the risky line.
  • throw against throws. One letter, two different jobs.
  • Catching a checked exception you never cause. Java refuses to compile a catch for a checked exception the try block cannot throw.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. State three differences between checked and unchecked exceptions.

2. Which exception does Integer.parseInt("abc") raise, and is it checked?

3. When does a finally block run?

4. Write the line that rejects an invalid day with an exception.
blocks.answer: 1. The compiler enforces checked ones but not unchecked; checked are known at compile time and unchecked only at run time; checked come from outside conditions and unchecked from program logic. 2. NumberFormatException, and it is unchecked. 3. Always, whether the try succeeded, threw, or returned. 4. throw new IllegalArgumentException("Day must be 1, 2 or 3");

blocks.big:
Checked: the compiler makes you deal with it, and it is the world's fault.
Unchecked: it does not, and it is your fault.
blocks.sub: try the risky bit, catch the one you expect, finally clean up. throw raises one, throws warns about one.

title: Reading and Writing Files
lead: The 2025/2026 paper called its file question "the file question, and the trick in its wording", and the trick is always the same: it asks you to add to a file you already created. One letter, one constructor argument, and the whole question turns on it.

blocks.label: What you must be able to do
blocks.html: Write records to a text file, add more without destroying what is there, read them all back, and handle the exception that file work forces you to handle.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line. Read a frame, do the small task,
then slide down to check.

frames.teach: Everything in variables disappears when the program stops. A file makes data outlive the run. Java gives you a writer and a reader, and the pleasant surprise is that the reader is one you already know.
frames.ask:
Which class have you used since Lesson 1.5 that can also read a
file?

frames.teach:
Point it at System.in and it reads the keyboard; point it at a File and it reads that file, with the same nextLine you already know. The writer is PrintWriter, and it has the same println you already know.

import java.io.PrintWriter;import java.io.File;import java.util.Scanner;import java.io.IOException;public class Files {    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("records.txt");        out.println("Ada, 72");        out.println("Victor, 65");        out.close();        Scanner in = new Scanner(new File("records.txt"));        while (in.hasNextLine()) {            System.out.println("read: " + in.nextLine());        }        in.close();    }}
Outputread: Ada, 72
read: Victor, 65
frames.ask: Find the one line that would lose your data if you deleted it.

frames.teach: Written text sits in a buffer until the writer is closed, so without it the file can be empty even though the program ran perfectly. Always close a writer.
frames.ask: What is in.hasNextLine() doing in the while?

frames.check:
Asking whether there is another line before trying to
take one.
frames.teach:
That is how you read a file of unknown length: keep going while there is
more. Now the trick.
frames.ask: What do you think happens if you open a file with new PrintWriter("log.txt") when log.txt already has data in it?

frames.check: It is wiped, instantly and silently.
frames.teach: PrintWriter on a filename always starts an empty file. That is right for creating records and catastrophic for adding to them, and it is precisely the error the paper plants.
frames.ask: So how do you add without destroying?

frames.check: Wrap a FileWriter with a second argument, true.
frames.teach:
That argument means append.

import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.PrintWriter;import java.io.File;import java.util.Scanner;import java.io.IOException;public class Appending {    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {        PrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("log.txt");        out.println("first line");        out.close();        PrintWriter more = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("log.txt", true));        more.println("second line, appended");        more.close();        Scanner in = new Scanner(new File("log.txt"));        while (in.hasNextLine()) {            System.out.println(in.nextLine());        }        in.close();    }}
Outputfirst line
second line, appended

Both lines survived. new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(name, true)) is the append form, and true is the whole difference.
frames.ask: Write both forms out, side by side, from memory.

frames.check: new PrintWriter(name) to create or overwrite; new PrintWriter(new FileWriter(name, true)) to append.
frames.teach: Last piece: the imports and the exception. File work raises checked exceptions, so the compiler insists.
frames.ask: What are your two options for satisfying it?

frames.check: Catch it, or declare throws IOException on the method.
frames.teach: The listings above declare it, which is shortest and perfectly acceptable in an exam. If the question asks you to handle a missing file gracefully, catch FileNotFoundException instead and print a message.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The four lines, and the one letter
blocks.html:
// imports, at the top of the fileimport java.io.PrintWriter;   import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.File;          import java.util.Scanner;import java.io.IOException;// CREATE or OVERWRITE: wipes anything already therePrintWriter out = new PrintWriter("records.txt");// APPEND: keeps what is there. The true is the whole differencePrintWriter out = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("records.txt", true));out.println("a record");out.close();                    // or the file may be empty// READ, line by line, however many there areScanner in = new Scanner(new File("records.txt"));while (in.hasNextLine()) {    String line = in.nextLine();}in.close();

The exception: file work throws checked exceptions, so every method that does it must either catch them or say throws IOException in its header.

The reading pattern for "display only the first five": count as you read and break at five, or read into an array or list and take the first five. Either earns the marks; counting is shorter.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html:
• Using new PrintWriter(name) for the append step. It wipes the file, and the question that asked you to add records without deleting the existing ones scores nothing. This is THE trap in this question.
  • Forgetting close(). The file can end up empty.
  • Forgetting the imports, especially java.io.File, which is separate from java.util.Scanner.
  • Opening a different filename later in the program. The paper insists the file created at the start is used for every later operation, so put the name in a variable and use that variable everywhere.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
1. Which constructor overwrites a file, and which appends to it?

2. What can happen if you forget close()?

3. Write the loop that reads every line of a file and prints it.

4. Why must a method that writes a file say throws IOException?
blocks.answer: 1. new PrintWriter("f.txt") overwrites; new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("f.txt", true)) appends. 2. The file may be left empty, because the text is still in a buffer. 3. while (in.hasNextLine()) { System.out.println(in.nextLine()); } 4. Because file operations raise checked exceptions, which the compiler requires you to catch or declare.

blocks.working:
Q1 a · define method overloading, and the role of the signature · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Method overloading is a feature that allows a class to have more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists (differing in the number, types, or order of parameters).

The method signature is a method's name together with its parameter list. Its role in resolution is this: at a call such as add(2, 3), the compiler compares the number, types and order of the arguments written at the call site against the parameter list of every candidate with that name, and selects the one whose signature matches (widening the argument types if no exact match exists). Because the resolution uses only what appears at the call site, and the return type is not part of the signature, the return type plays no role: two methods differing only by return type are rejected by the compiler as a duplicate definition. The choice is therefore made entirely at compile time, which is why overloading is called compile-time (static) polymorphism.

Where the marks are: one for the definition, one for "signature = name + parameter list" and the fact that the return type is excluded. Saying "the compiler picks the right one" without saying how is half an answer. See Units 5.1 and 5.6.

Q1 b · three differences: checked vs unchecked · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. When they are detected. Checked exceptions are checked by the compiler at compile time; unchecked exceptions occur at run time and the compiler does not examine them.
  2. Whether you must handle them. A checked exception must be either caught in a try-catch or declared with throws, or the code will not compile. An unchecked exception carries no such obligation.
  3. What causes them. Checked exceptions represent conditions outside the program's control (a missing file, a failed network call), whereas unchecked exceptions represent programming errors (dereferencing null, a bad index, dividing by zero).

Examples (add them; they cost one line and prove the point): checked: IOException, FileNotFoundException, ClassNotFoundException. Unchecked: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ArithmeticException.

Where the marks are: three distinct axes. Writing "one is checked and one is not" three different ways scores one mark. See Unit 10.1.

Q1 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

Read the output first. "141.0" tells you the sum is a double before you have read a line of code. That single character finds two of the five errors.

Code · the paper's snippet, with every error marked · AS PRINTED
import javax.swing.JOptionPane;public class Snippet {public static void main(String[] args) {int[] arr = {24.0, 40.0, 66.0, 80.0, 98.0};        // ERROR 1 and 2  int sum = 0;                                     // ERROR 2  int matches = 0;  boolean stop = false;  for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length && !stop; i++) {   // ERROR 3      for (int j = i; j < arr.length; j++) {          if (arr[j] % 4 == 0) {                     // ERROR 4              continue;          }          sum += arr[j] - j;                        // ERROR 5          matches++;          if (matches == 3) {              stop = true;          }          break;      }  }  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Sum: " + sum);  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Matches: " + matches);  System.exit(0);}}
Worked example · The five errors, and why each is one
  1. Line 4: int[] cannot hold 24.0. Those are double literals. This is a compile error: "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int". Fix: double[] arr. The output confirms it: 141.0 is a double.
  2. Line 5: int sum cannot total doubles, and could never print "141.0". Fix: double sum = 0; Unit 3.3: the type decides what you may do and how it prints.
  3. Line 8: i <= arr.length is off by one. Indexes run 0 to length-1 (F.10). Fix: i < arr.length. Here it would not actually throw, because the inner loop never runs when i = 5, but it is still wrong and it is one of the five marks.
  4. Lines 10 to 12: the continue is inverted. The spec says find numbers that are multiples of 4. This skips them and processes everything else: precisely backwards. Fix: if (arr[j] % 4 != 0) continue; Unit 4.7: read every continue as "unless". This is the error worth the most attention, because it is the one that is pure logic.
  5. Line 13: arr[j] - j subtracts the index. The spec says add (that number - 1). Fix: sum += arr[j] - 1; A subtle one: with j it would give the right answer for j = 1 only, so a spot check could miss it.
Code · corrected, and it reproduces the paper's answer · VERIFIED ON THE JVM

The answer. Compute each digit cubed (all five are 3-digit numbers, so the power is 3):

Q1 d ii · convert the loops · 10 MARKS, PART TWO

Read it precisely. The original has three loops:

LoopCurrentlyBecomes
the outer one over idxforwhile
counting the digitswhilefor
summing the powerswhilefor
the inner p loopforwhile

"The For Loop" (singular) is the outer one; "the While loops" (plural) are the two digit loops. The innermost p loop is also a for, so convert it too: the safest reading is that every for becomes a while and every while becomes a for. Apply Unit 4.6's recipe to each.

Code · every loop converted, same output · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class ArmstrongConverted {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] numbers = {370, 371, 372, 407, 408};        // FOR -> WHILE: init out, condition in, update at the bottom        int idx = 0;        while (idx < numbers.length) {            int n = numbers[idx], digits = 0, temp = n, sum = 0;            // WHILE -> FOR: no init needed, temp is the counter            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                digits++;            }            temp = n;            // WHILE -> FOR            for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) {                int d = temp % 10, power = 1;                // FOR -> WHILE                int p = 0;                while (p < digits) {                    power *= d;                    p++;                }                sum += power;            }            System.out.println(n + " -> "                + (sum == n ? "ARMSTRONG" : "NOT ARMSTRONG"));            idx++;                      // the update, at the bottom        }    }}
Output370 -> ARMSTRONG
371 -> ARMSTRONG
372 -> NOT ARMSTRONG
407 -> ARMSTRONG
408 -> NOT ARMSTRONG

Identical output to the original. That is the test of a conversion: same program, different clothes.

Two points a marker looks for. The for (; temp > 0; temp /= 10) has an empty initialisation, which is legal and is the honest conversion: the original while had nothing to initialise, because temp already existed. Do not invent a variable to fill the slot. And idx++ sits at the bottom of the while body, which is Unit 4.6's step 3 and the one people forget: leave it out and the program runs forever.

Q2 a · define encapsulation · 2 MARKS

Model answer.

Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on them into a single unit (a class), while restricting direct access to some of its components.

In Java it is achieved by declaring the fields private and exposing controlled access through public getter and setter methods. This gives data hiding (unauthorised code cannot read or modify the state), validation (a setter can reject invalid input, for example preventing a negative balance), and flexibility (the internal representation can change without breaking any code that uses the class).

Where the marks are: one for the bundling-plus- restricting definition, one for how it is achieved (private fields, public getters and setters). Add one benefit if you have room. See Unit 6.4.

Q2 b · three differences: overloading vs overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer. Three differences, one mark each:

  1. Where they occur. Overloading happens within a single class: several methods share a name. Overriding happens between a superclass and a subclass: the subclass replaces the inherited method.
  2. The parameter list. Overloaded methods must have different parameter lists. An overriding method must have exactly the same name and parameter list as the one it overrides.
  3. When the method is chosen. Overloading is resolved at compile time by the compiler (static polymorphism); overriding is resolved at run time by the JVM, from the object's actual type (dynamic polymorphism).

Where the marks are: three separate axes. If you have room, add that overriding requires inheritance and overloading does not. See Unit 6.7.

Q2 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

The same five errors as Q1, in the same order. This is the payoff of the template.

Worked example · The five errors
  1. Line 4: int[] prices = {15.5, ...}. Decimal literals in an int array: a compile error. Fix: double[] prices. The output "202.725" says double before you read anything else.
  2. Line 5: int total = 0; cannot hold 202.725. Fix: double total = 0;
  3. Line 8: i <= prices.length is off by one. Fix: i < prices.length. Unlike Q1, this one would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at i = 6, because line 9 reads prices[i] straight away. Same error, worse consequence.
  4. Line 9: if (prices[i] > 20) continue; is inverted. The spec says skip anything under 20. This skips everything over 20, i.e. exactly the items to be discounted. Fix: if (prices[i] < 20) continue;
  5. Line 15: if (count == 5). The spec says stop once 4 have been discounted. Fix: if (count == 4). Only four of the six prices are 20 or above anyway, so with == 5 the flag never fires. The count would still be 4, and the total would still be right, which makes this the easiest error to miss: it does not change the answer, it just means the code does not do what it was asked.

Q2 d i · state the output · 10 MARKS, PART ONE

The answer: Perfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23

The reasoning, which is worth writing out because "no need to show workings" does not mean "do not check":

ClassCountWhich
Perfect26 (1+2+3 = 6) and 28 (1+2+4+7+14 = 28)
Abundant512 (16), 18 (21), 20 (22), 24 (36), 30 (42)
Deficient23everything else, including every prime, and 1

Two checks that catch mistakes. 2 + 5 + 23 = 30, so every number is classified exactly once. And 1 is deficient: its proper divisors sum to 0, because 1 has no proper divisor, and the loop for (div = 1; div < num; div++) never runs for num = 1. Forget that and you get 22, not 23.

Code · confirmed, with the classification printed · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        for (int num = 1; num <= 30; num++) {            int sum = 0;            for (int div = 1; div < num; div++) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);        System.out.println("check: " + (perfectCount + abundantCount + deficientCount)            + " numbers classified");    }}
OutputPerfect: 2, Abundant: 5, Deficient: 23
check: 30 numbers classified
Code · q2 d ii · for loops converted to while loops · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class NumberClassifierWhile {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int perfectCount = 0, abundantCount = 0, deficientCount = 0;        int num = 1;                        // 1. init above        while (num <= 30) {                 // 2. condition            int sum = 0;            int div = 1;                    // the inner one too            while (div < num) {                if (num % div == 0) sum += div;                div++;                      // 3. update at the bottom            }            if (sum == num) perfectCount++;            else if (sum > num) abundantCount++;            else deficientCount++;            num++;                          // 3. update at the bottom        }        System.out.println("Perfect: " + perfectCount + ", Abundant: " + abundantCount            + ", Deficient: " + deficientCount);    }}

Identical output, which is the whole test. Note int sum = 0; stays inside the outer loop: it must be reset for every number, and moving it out is the classic way to wreck this conversion. The recipe only moves the loop's own three parts; everything else stays exactly where it was, which is what "retain other things" means.

Q3 a · consecutive duplicates in a sales log · 12 MARKS

Write a program that (i) counts, in one pass, the indices i >= 1 where the amount equals the one before it; (ii) returns a single String listing, in order and comma separated, every amount that equals its predecessor or its successor, built with plain String concatenation only; (iii) displays both in one JOptionPane dialog. The paper adds a hint: it must not flag 35, 15, or 25.

Must memorise · Parts i and ii count DIFFERENT things

Part i counts positions. Part ii lists values. They are not the same question asked twice, and they do not give the same number.

Part i asks how many boundaries have a twin across them. Part ii asks which elements are touching a twin at all.

Look at the three 40s. They contain two boundaries (index 3 to 4, and 4 to 5) but three elements. So part i counts 2 there and part ii lists 3. Read the two parts as one question and you will answer one of them wrong.

MEMORY HOOK: fences and posts. Part i counts the fences between posts, part ii counts the posts. A run of n twins has n posts and n-1 fences, always.

Dry run · Both answers, by hand, before writing any code

Check it against the hint. The paper told you 35, 15 and 25 must not be flagged, and they are the only three that are not. The examiner has handed you a way to test your own trace before you write a line of code, which is exactly what the hint is for.

And check the two answers against each other. The runs are 20-20 (2 long), 40-40-40 (3 long) and 60-60 (2 long). Part ii flags 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 values. Part i counts 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 positions. They differ by exactly 3, the number of runs, because each run loses one to the fences-and-posts rule. If your two answers do not differ by the number of runs, one of them is wrong.

Code · question three, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SalesDuplicates {    // Part i: ONE pass. Count every index i >= 1 whose amount equals the one before.    static int countConsecutiveDuplicates(int[] sales) {        int count = 0;        for (int i = 1; i < sales.length; i++) {            if (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]) {                count++;            }        }        return count;    }    // Part ii: every amount equal to its predecessor OR its successor, in order,    // comma separated, built with plain String concatenation only.    static String flaggedAmounts(int[] sales) {        String result = "";        for (int i = 0; i < sales.length; i++) {            boolean sameAsPrevious = (i > 0) && (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]);            boolean sameAsNext = (i < sales.length - 1) && (sales[i] == sales[i + 1]);            if (sameAsPrevious || sameAsNext) {                if (result.equals("")) {                    result = "" + sales[i];                } else {                    result = result + ", " + sales[i];                }            }        }        return result;    }    // Part iii: one dialog showing both answers.    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] saleAmounts = {20, 20, 35, 40, 40, 40, 15, 60, 60, 25};        int duplicates = countConsecutiveDuplicates(saleAmounts);        String flagged = flaggedAmounts(saleAmounts);        String message = "Consecutive duplicate count: " + duplicates                       + "\nFlagged amounts: " + flagged;        System.out.println(message);    }}

Flagged amounts: 20, 20, 40, 40, 40, 60, 60

Exactly the hand trace, including the three amounts the paper told us not to flag. The dialog is a println here so its text can be printed in this book; in the hall, write JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, message); and import javax.swing.JOptionPane (F.11).

Trap · Three ways to lose marks on part A

1. Starting part i's loop at 0. The question says i >= 1, and for a reason: sales[0 - 1] is sales[-1], which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (Unit 8.1). Index 0 has no predecessor, so the loop starts at 1. This is where "one pass" is easiest to get right and easiest to throw away.

2. Forgetting the boundary guards in part ii. Index 0 has no predecessor and the last index has no successor. The guards (i > 0) and (i < sales.length - 1) are what stop the reads from running off either end. They work because && is short-circuit (Unit 3.6): when i > 0 is false, Java never evaluates sales[i - 1], so it never throws. Swap the two sides of the && and the program crashes on the first element.

3. The leading comma. Concatenating ", " + sales[i] every time gives , 20, 20, 40... with a comma stuck on the front. The test if (result.equals("")) writes the first value bare and every later value with its separator in front. Compare Strings with .equals(), never with == (Unit 7.3).

The question bans StringBuilder deliberately: it wants to see that you can handle the separator yourself. Use StringBuilder anyway and you have answered a question the paper did not ask.

Q3 b · student records with basic file i/o · 13 MARKS
  1. creates input.txt and writes at least three students (ID, name, CGPA) into it with FileWriter, one per line, wrapped in try-catch;
  2. reads student details from output.txt with FileReader and prints each line exactly as it appears, handling any exception including the case where output.txt does not exist;
  3. has a method that takes a file name, counts the lines, and returns the count, handling its own exceptions internally;
  4. closes every resource, and prints a clear, specific message in every catch block.
Must memorise · It writes input.txt and reads output.txt

Part 1 writes input.txt. Part 2 reads output.txt. The program never creates output.txt.

That is not a misprint for you to tidy up. It is the question.

Read part 2 again: "handle any exception that may occur while reading, including the case where output.txt does not exist." The examiner has told you, in the question itself, that the file will be missing. The marks are for the catch block running, not for the file being read.

So do not "fix" it by reading input.txt instead. Write exactly what the paper asks, and let the catch block do its job. That is the answer.

MEMORY HOOK: the missing file is the exam. When a question names a file it never created, the catch block is the thing being marked.

Teach · The five classes, and why the list is exactly these five

The restriction looks arbitrary. It is not: the five are exactly what you need and nothing more (Unit 10.3).

ClassDirectionWhat it is for
FileWriteroutWrites characters to a file. On its own it writes one character at a time.
BufferedWriteroutWraps a FileWriter and collects characters, writing them in blocks. Also gives you newLine().
FileReaderinReads characters from a file. On its own it reads one character at a time: it has no readLine().
BufferedReaderinWraps a FileReader and gives you readLine(), which is the whole reason it is on the list.
IOException-The checked exception every one of the above can throw. You must catch it or declare it (Unit 10.1).

The pairing is the point. The question says "read using FileReader" and "one student per line". A FileReader alone cannot give you a line. So you wrap it: new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName)). That is why both appear on the list, and it is why the list is not padding.

And read "or its subclasses" carefully. Those three words are permission. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, so you are explicitly allowed to catch it separately, which is exactly how you answer part 2's "including the case where output.txt does not exist" with a message that says what actually happened.

Trap · Catch the child before the parent, or it will not compile

When you catch both, the subclass must come first. Java tries catch blocks top to bottom and takes the first that fits. Put IOException first and it swallows everything, leaving the FileNotFoundException block unreachable. Java does not let that pass:

import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.IOException;public class CatchOrder {    public static void main(String[] args) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("any.txt"))) {            System.out.println(in.readLine());        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("the parent is caught first");        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("this line can never run");        }    }}
Compiler outputerror: exception FileNotFoundException has already been caught

This is one of Java's friendlier errors: it refuses to compile code containing a block that could never run. Reverse the two catch blocks and it compiles. Specific first, general last, every time.

Code · question three, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.io.BufferedReader;import java.io.BufferedWriter;import java.io.FileNotFoundException;import java.io.FileReader;import java.io.FileWriter;import java.io.IOException;public class StudentRecords {    // Part i: create input.txt and write three student records, one per line.    static void writeStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedWriter out = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(fileName))) {            out.write("STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78");            out.newLine();            out.write("STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92");            out.newLine();            System.out.println("Wrote 3 student records to " + fileName);        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Could not write to " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part ii: read a file and print every line exactly as it appears.    static void printStudents(String fileName) {        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            String line = in.readLine();            while (line != null) {                System.out.println(line);                line = in.readLine();            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot read " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while reading " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());        }    }    // Part iii: count a file's records. Handles its own exceptions; never throws.    static int countRecords(String fileName) {        int lines = 0;        try (BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(fileName))) {            while (in.readLine() != null) {                lines++;            }        } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {            System.out.println("Cannot count " + fileName                + ": the file does not exist.");            return -1;        } catch (IOException e) {            System.out.println("Error while counting " + fileName + ": "                + e.getMessage());            return -1;        }        return lines;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        writeStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper " +            "asks ---");        printStudents("output.txt");        System.out.println("--- the same method on the file we did write ---");        printStudents("input.txt");        System.out.println("--- part iii: counting records ---");        System.out.println("input.txt holds " + countRecords("input.txt")            + " records");        System.out.println("output.txt holds " + countRecords("output.txt")            + " records");    }}
OutputWrote 3 student records to input.txt
--- part ii: reading output.txt, exactly as the paper asks ---
Cannot read output.txt: the file does not exist.
--- the same method on the file we did write ---
STU001, Ada Bello, 4.51
STU002, Femi Okonkwo, 3.78
STU003, Ngozi Eze, 4.92
--- part iii: counting records ---
input.txt holds 3 records
Cannot count output.txt: the file does not exist.
output.txt holds -1 records

Line 3 of that output is the 13 marks. The program did exactly what the paper asked, the file was not there, and the catch block said so in words a human can read.

Teach · Four decisions in that program worth defending

1. try-with-resources answers part 4 on its own. Writing try (BufferedWriter out = ...) closes the writer automatically, whether the block ends normally or throws (Unit 10.2). The paper allows a finally block instead, and it is worth knowing why the bracket form is better: a close() inside finally can itself throw, and if it does while an earlier exception is already travelling, the second exception replaces the first and the real cause disappears. If you do use finally, the close must sit inside its own try-catch, and it must test for null, because the resource may have failed to open at all.

2. Wrapping means closing one thing, not two. out.close() on the BufferedWriter closes the FileWriter inside it. Closing the wrapper closes what it wraps, so one bracket handles both.

3. countRecords returns -1, not 0, when it fails. The method must "handle its own exceptions internally", so it cannot throw, so it must return something. Return 0 and the caller cannot tell a missing file from an empty one. -1 is impossible as a line count, so it can only mean failure. A value chosen because it cannot be mistaken for a real answer is called a sentinel, and picking a good one is a real skill.

4. Read the last two lines of the output in the right order. "Cannot count output.txt" prints before "output.txt holds -1 records", even though the second is the println that contains the first as an argument. Java evaluates the arguments before it calls the method: countRecords runs to completion, printing its own message, and only then does the outer println receive -1 and print. Argument first, call second, always.

Q4 · inheritance and polymorphism · 25 MARKS

Part 1, BankAccount (9 marks). Private fields for account number, holder name and balance; a constructor initialising all three; a method that adds to the balance; a method that deducts if funds suffice and otherwise rejects with a message; a method that displays the details.

Part 2, subclasses (10 marks). SavingAccount overrides the withdrawal so it is allowed only if the balance after the withdrawal would still be >= 1000. CurrentAccount overrides it so every successful withdrawal adds a 50 reward afterwards.

Part 3, main (6 marks). One of each; deposit into each; at least one successful and one unsuccessful or reward-triggering withdrawal on each; details before and after; and demonstrate polymorphism by storing each object in a BankAccount reference and calling the withdrawal through it, confirming the correct overridden version runs.

Must memorise · The question contains a contradiction, and resolving it is the exam

Part 1 says the balance must be private.

Part 2 says the subclasses must change the balance.

A private field is invisible to a subclass. So the subclass cannot touch it.

This is not the examiner being careless. It is the whole of Units 6.4 and 6.6 arriving in one question: encapsulation says the field is private, and inheritance says the child must still be able to work with it. The way out is the only way out, and it is the answer being marked: the subclass goes through the parent's public methods, using getBalance() to read and super.withdraw(amount) or deposit(amount) to change.

MEMORY HOOK: the child knocks, it does not climb in through the window. getBalance() to look, super.withdraw() to act.

Trap · A subclass cannot see a private field, and it will say so

The tempting move is to write the arithmetic straight into the subclass. Java stops you at the compiler:

class Account {    private double balance = 5000;}class Saving extends Account {    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        balance = balance - amount;        return true;    }}public class SubclassReach {    public static void main(String[] args) {        new Saving().withdraw(100);    }}
Compiler outputerror: balance has private access in Account

Private means the declaring class only, and a subclass is a different class. Inheritance gives Saving the field (every Saving object really does contain a balance) but not access to it. The field is there and untouchable, which is exactly what private is for (Unit 6.4).

Would protected fix it? It would compile, and it is the wrong answer here, because part 1 said private. Marks are for doing what the question said. Beyond the exam, going through the parent's methods is better anyway: every rule the parent enforces on a withdrawal keeps being enforced. Make the field protected and each subclass has to remember those rules for itself, which is how a bank ends up with an account that can be overdrawn down one code path and not another. See the access table in Unit 6.6.

Teach · Why withdraw returns boolean

The paper does not say what withdraw returns, and the obvious choice is void. Then read part 2 ii again: a CurrentAccount adds the reward on every successful withdrawal. Not on every attempt. So the override has to know whether the withdrawal succeeded, and a void method tells it nothing.

Making withdraw return boolean makes the override three honest lines:

boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);if (succeeded) { deposit(50); }return succeeded;

The alternative, comparing the balance before and after, works but is worse: it re-derives an answer the parent already knew and threw away. When a method knows something the caller needs, it should return it. Notice that this decision is forced by a single word in part 2 ii, which is what "read the question" means in practice.

Code · question four, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// ===== Part 1: the superclass =====class BankAccount {    private String accountNumber;    private String holderName;    private double balance;    // Part 1 i: a constructor that initialises all three fields.    public BankAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        this.accountNumber = accountNumber; }    public String getHolderName()    { return holderName; }    public double getBalance()       { return balance; }    // Part 1 ii: add a given amount to the balance.    public void deposit(double amount) {        balance = balance + amount;
