           System.out.println("Withdraw " + amount + " -> " + accountNumber                + " balance is now " + balance);            return true;        }        System.out.println("REJECTED: " + accountNumber + " holds only " + balance            + ", so " + amount + " cannot be withdrawn"); " +                "Withdrawing "                + amount + " from " + getAccountNumber() + " would leave "                + (getBalance() - amount));            return false;        }        return super.withdraw(amount);    }}// ===== Part 2 ii: every successful withdrawal earns a 50 reward =====class CurrentAccount extends BankAccount {    public CurrentAccount(String accountNumber, String holderName, double balance) {        super(accountNumber, holderName, balance);    }    @Override    public boolean withdraw(double amount) {        boolean succeeded = super.withdraw(amount);        if (succeeded) {            System.out.println("Reward earned on " + getAccountNumber() + ":");            deposit(50);        }        return succeeded;    }}// ===== Part 3: the main method =====public class BankSystem {    public static void main(String[] args) {        // Part 3 i: at least one of each. System.out.println("=== ii: deposit into each ===");        saving.deposit(2000.0);        current.deposit(1000.0);        // Part 3 iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on each.        System.out.println("=== iii: a successful and an unsuccessful withdrawal on " +            "each ===");        saving.withdraw(4000.0);        saving.withdraw(2500.0);        current.withdraw(1000.0);        current.withdraw(999999.0);        System.out.println("=== iv: details AFTER the transactions ===");        saving.displayDetails();        current.displayDetails();        // Part 3 v: polymorphism. Same reference type, same call, same amount.        System.out.println("=== v: polymorphism, same reference type, same call, " +            "same amount ===");        BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();        acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);        acc.withdraw(600.0);        acc.displayDetails();    }}

All four classes live in one file because only one may be public and that one must match the file name: BankSystem.java. In the hall, write them as four classes exactly as they are here, or as four separate files. Both are correct.

Dry run · Every balance, and why each rule fired
Callbalance beforewhich rule decidedallowed?balance after
SA-1001, a SavingAccount, opens at 5000
deposit(2000)5000.0no rule: deposits always landyes7000.0
withdraw(4000)7000.07000 - 4000 = 3000, and 3000 >= 1000yes3000.0
withdraw(2500)3000.03000 - 2500 = 500, and 500 < 1000no3000.0
CA-2002, a CurrentAccount, opens at 3000
deposit(1000)3000.0no ruleyes4000.0
withdraw(1000)4000.0funds suffice, so the reward firesyes3000.0, then +50 = 3050.0
withdraw(999999)3050.0funds do not suffice, so no rewardno3050.0

The last row is the one to study. The reward sits inside if (succeeded), so a rejected withdrawal earns nothing. Had withdraw returned void, that if could not have been written, and CA-2002 would have been paid 50 for a transaction that never happened.

Must memorise · How to prove polymorphism in six lines

Part 3 v asks you to confirm the correct overridden version runs. A proof needs a control: change one thing and show the behaviour changes.

So: same reference type, same method, same amount, same starting balance. Only the object differs.

BankAccount acc = new SavingAccount("SA-3003", "Ngozi Eze", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // rejected: would leave 900, under 1000acc = new CurrentAccount("CA-4004", "Tunde Ade", 1500.0);acc.withdraw(600.0);        // allowed, and pays a 50 reward: 950

Both variables are declared BankAccount. Both calls are acc.withdraw(600.0), character for character. Both accounts hold 1500.0. One is refused and one is paid a bonus.

That is the proof, and here is the sentence that earns the mark: the compiler only knew acc was a BankAccount, so the choice of which withdraw to run could not have been made at compile time. It was made at run time, from the object's actual class. That is dynamic method dispatch, and it is what "polymorphism" names (Unit 6.7).

MEMORY HOOK: the reference decides what you may call. The object decides what actually runs.

Compare this with the TRAP at the end of Unit 6.6, where the same setup silently ran the parent's method because the override was really an overload. Same two lines of code, opposite outcomes, and the difference was one parameter type. That is why @Override sits on every override here.

(12 marks)A. A conference organiser needs a program (using JOptionPane only, for all input/output) that prices tickets for a 3-day conference and produces a sales summary. Implement the following four methods.

i.    Create a method that takes in a day number. Use a switch statement to return a base ticket price for Day 1, Day 2, or Day 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly). If the day number is not 1, 2, or 3, throw an IllegalArgumentException.

ii.   Create a method that takes in a tier and a number of days attending. Use nested if-else statements (not a switch, and not independent/separate if checks) to return a discount percentage:

•  Gold, attending all 3 days -> 25%

•  Gold, attending 1-2 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending all 3 days -> 15%

•  Silver, attending 1-2 days -> 5%

•  Bronze (any days) -> 0%

•  Any tier string that is not "Gold" or "Silver" must be treated as "Bronze"

The nesting must reflect that "days attending" is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check.

iii.  Create a method that takes in a base price total and a discount percentage and applies the discount to the base price total. If the discounted amount is below 50.0, the method should return 50.0 instead (a price floor).

iv.  main()

•  Ask the user for the number of attendees N (a positive integer).

•  Loop exactly N times. In each iteration, ask for that attendee's number of days attending (an integer from 1 to 3, inclusive) and tier. For each day from 1 up to that attendee's days attending, call the method from part (i) and add the result to that attendee's running base price total (a running total that starts at 0 for each new attendee). Then call the method from part (ii) to get the discount percentage, and the method from part (iii) to get that attendee's final price.

•  Accumulate: (a) total revenue across all attendees, and (b) a running count of how many attendees were Gold, Silver, and Bronze.

v.   After the loop, show one summary dialog with total revenue and the three tier counts.

Q5 a · conference ticket pricing · 12 MARKS
  1. takes a day number, uses a switch to return a base price for Day 1, 2 or 3 (pick any three distinct prices and state them clearly); any other day throws IllegalArgumentException;

The nesting must reflect that days are only checked within each tier branch;
  3. takes a base total and a discount percentage, applies it, and returns 50.0 if the result would fall below 50.0 (a price floor);
  4. main(): ask for N attendees; loop N times asking days and tier; sum the day prices into a per-attendee base total; get the discount; get the final price; accumulate total revenue and a count of Gold, Silver and Bronze; then show one summary dialog.
Must memorise · Choose prices that let the floor fire

The question lets you pick the three prices. That freedom is a trap with a right answer.

Pick 15000, 12000 and 9000 and part 3's price floor can never fire. The largest possible discount is 25%, so nothing ever falls near 50.0. You will have written a floor you cannot demonstrate and the examiner cannot see work.

Pick 30.0, 25.0 and 20.0 and the floor becomes live: one Gold day is 30, less 15% is 25.50, which is below 50.0, so the method returns 50.0. The 50.0 floor is itself the hint about the scale the examiner had in mind.

MEMORY HOOK: when a question lets you choose the numbers, choose numbers that make every rule visible. A rule that never fires is a rule you cannot be shown to have written correctly.

Teach · What "nested, not separate" actually means here

Part 2 is unusually explicit: nested if-else, not a switch, not independent if checks, and "the nesting must reflect that days attending is only checked within each tier branch, not as a separate top-level check."

So the shape is forced. The tier decides the branch; the days are examined inside it:

What the question demandsWhat loses the mark
if (Gold) { if (days == 3) 25 else 15 }
else if (Silver) { if (days == 3) 15 else 5 }
else { 0 }		 if (Gold && days == 3) 25;
if (Gold && days < 3) 15;
if (Silver && days == 3) 15;
Right answers, wrong structure: days is tested at the top level, four separate times. This is what "not independent checks" forbids.

Why the final else is the whole Bronze rule. "Any tier string that is not Gold or Silver must be treated as Bronze" is not an extra check you add: it is what a bare else already means. Write else if (tier.equals("Bronze")) and you have broken the rule, because "Platinum" would then match nothing and fall through with no discount assigned. The bare else catches Bronze, Platinum, "gold" in lower case, and an empty string, which is exactly what was asked (Unit 4.4).

The same else must also do the counting. If "Platinum" is treated as Bronze for the discount, it is a Bronze attendee in the summary too. Count it anywhere else and your dialog contradicts your own pricing.

Code · question five, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ConferenceTickets {    // Part i: a switch returning the base price for a day. Any other day is illegal.    static double basePriceForDay(int day) {        switch (day) {            case 1:  return 30.0;            case 2:  return 25.0;            case 3:  return 20.0;            default: throw new IllegalArgumentException(                         "Day must be 1, 2 or 3 but was " + day);        }    }    // Part ii: NESTED if-else. Days are only examined inside a tier branch.    static double discountPercent(String tier, int daysAttending) {        if (tier.equals("Gold")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 25.0;            } else {                return 15.0;            }        } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {            if (daysAttending == 3) {                return 15.0;            } else {                return 5.0;            }        } else {            return 0.0;        }    }    // Part iii: apply the discount, with a price floor of 50.0.    static double applyDiscount(double baseTotal, double percent) {        double discounted = baseTotal - (baseTotal * percent / 100.0);        if (discounted < 50.0) {            return 50.0;        }        return discounted;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int attendees = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        double totalRevenue = 0;        int goldCount = 0, silverCount = 0, bronzeCount = 0;        for (int a = 1; a <= attendees; a++) {            int days = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            String tier = in.nextLine();            double baseTotal = 0;            for (int d = 1; d <= days; d++) {                baseTotal += basePriceForDay(d);            }            double percent = discountPercent(tier, days);            double finalPrice = applyDiscount(baseTotal, percent);            totalRevenue += finalPrice;            if (tier.equals("Gold")) {                goldCount++;            } else if (tier.equals("Silver")) {                silverCount++;            } else {                bronzeCount++;            }            System.out.println("Attendee " + a + ": " + tier + ", " + days                + " day(s), base "                + baseTotal + ", discount " + percent + "%, pays " + finalPrice);        }        System.out.println("SUMMARY");        System.out.println("Total revenue: " + totalRevenue);        System.out.println("Gold: " + goldCount + ", Silver: " + silverCount            + ", Bronze: " + bronzeCount);    }}

Attendee 2: Gold, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 15.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 3: Silver, 2 day(s), base 55.0, discount 5.0%, pays 52.25
Attendee 4: Bronze, 1 day(s), base 30.0, discount 0.0%, pays 50.0
Attendee 5: Platinum, 3 day(s), base 75.0, discount 0.0%, pays 75.0
SUMMARY

Gold: 2, Silver: 1, Bronze: 2

Read attendees 2 and 4: both would have paid less than 50 and both paid exactly 50.0, so the floor is visibly working. Read attendee 5: "Platinum" got a 0% discount and was counted as Bronze, so the two Bronze rules agree. Input is a Scanner here so the run can be printed; in the hall, every prompt is JOptionPane.showInputDialog and the summary is one showMessageDialog (F.11).

Trap · The switch must return, or fall through

Part 1's method must give back a price for 1, 2 and 3 and throw otherwise. Writing return inside each case is what makes that safe: a return leaves the method immediately, so no break is needed and there is no fall-through to worry about (Unit 4.3).

Use double price; with assignments instead and you must not forget the breaks, and the compiler will additionally complain that price "might not have been initialized" unless every path assigns it. The default: throw is what convinces the compiler every path is covered: an exception is a legitimate way to leave a method that promised to return a double, because it does not return at all.

Note also that throw needs no throws clause here. IllegalArgumentException is unchecked (Unit 10.1), which is Q1 B's distinction being examined a second time on the same paper.

Q5 b · sustained breaches of a safe limit · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt 24 times, one dialog per hour. Each input must parse as a number between -20 and 50 inclusive; if invalid, re-prompt for the same hour using a nested loop, until valid. Store all 24 in a 1-D array;
  2. scan the array once, using only loops and conditionals (no extra arrays), to find the number of qualifying streaks (runs of 3 or more consecutive breach-hours) and the length of the longest breach streak;
  3. using nested if-else, classify: CRITICAL if the longest streak is >= 6, WARNING if it is 3 to 5, SAFE if no streak of 3 or more occurred;
  4. show one dialog with the streak count, the longest length, and the classification.
Must memorise · Count the run when it turns 3, and measure it as you go

The whole of part 2 is three variables and one pass:

currentRun: breach hours in a row right now, reset to 0 on any non-breach.
longestStreak: updated every breach hour, not at the end of a run.
qualifyingStreaks: incremented when currentRun == 3, exactly.

Why == 3 and not >= 3. A run passes through 3 exactly once, on its third hour. So == 3 counts each qualifying run once, however long it becomes. Use >= 3 and a 6-hour run is counted four times, giving 4 streaks where there is one.

MEMORY HOOK: a run is counted at the moment it qualifies, not while it continues. The threshold is a door you pass through once, not a room you stay in.

Trap · The streak that is still running when the day ends

The instinct is to close each run in the else, where the non-breach hour is: "the run just ended, so now measure it."

if (readings[hour] > 8) {    currentRun++;} else {    if (currentRun > longestStreak) longestStreak = currentRun;  // non-breach only    if (currentRun >= 3) qualifyingStreaks++;    currentRun = 0;}

It works, until the day ends mid-streak. If hours 18 to 23 are all breaches, the loop finishes with currentRun = 6 and never reaches the else. The longest streak of the day is never measured and never counted. The program reports SAFE on a day the freezer was over temperature for six straight hours.

The fix is not to bolt a copy of the else-block on after the loop. That is the usual patch and it duplicates the logic in two places, so the next edit changes one and forgets the other. Instead, update on every breach hour:

Measure longestStreak as the run grows, and count the run the instant it turns 3. Then a run that is still going when the array ends has already been measured and already been counted, and the end of the array needs no special case at all.

This is worth more than one exam question. A boundary you never treat specially cannot be got wrong at the boundary.

Code · question five, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ColdStorage {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        double[] readings = new double[24];        // Part i: 24 prompts, each re-prompted until the value is valid.        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            boolean valid = false;            while (!valid) {                String typed = in.nextLine();                try {                    double t = Double.parseDouble(typed);                    if (t >= -20 && t <= 50) {                        readings[hour] = t;                        valid = true;                    } else {                        System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": " + t                            + " is outside -20 to 50. Asking again.");                    }                } catch (NumberFormatException e) {                    System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": \"" + typed                        + "\" is not a number. Asking again.");                }            }        }        // Part ii: ONE scan, no extra arrays.        int currentRun = 0, longestStreak = 0, qualifyingStreaks = 0;        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            if (readings[hour] > 8) {                currentRun++;                if (currentRun > longestStreak) {                    longestStreak = currentRun;                }                if (currentRun == 3) {                    qualifyingStreaks++;                }            } else {                currentRun = 0;            }        }        // Part iii: classify.        String classification;        if (longestStreak >= 6) {            classification = "CRITICAL";        } else if (longestStreak >= 3) {            classification = "WARNING";        } else {            classification = "SAFE";        }        // Part iv: one dialog.        String message = "Qualifying streaks (3+ hours): " + qualifyingStreaks                       + "\nLongest breach streak: " + longestStreak + " hour(s)"                       + "\nClassification: " + classification;        System.out.println(message);    }}

The run fed hour 0 a 99, then the text "abc", then a valid 5, so both halves of "must parse as a number between -20 and 50" are shown rejecting input and re-prompting the same hour.

Dry run · The 24 hours, and where the three streaks are
breach = above 8. The bar shows breach hours.

The first run of 2 is the control: it proves the counter is not simply counting runs. The last run is the trap above, live: it reaches hour 23 and stops because the day stopped, not because the temperature did. It is both the longest streak and the one that decides the classification, and the else-branch version would have missed it entirely and printed WARNING.

(12 marks)A. Design and implement a program, using JOptionPane only for input and output, that classifies a single user-supplied positive integer N according to its digit pattern (Palindrome).

Definition: A number is a palindrome if it reads the same forwards and backwards (i.e. it is equal to its own digit-reversed value). For example, 4884 and 7 are palindromes; 4821 is not.

Constraints: The entire task must be implemented inside main() only, using loops and nested/chained if-else and/or switch logic. No arrays and no user-defined helper methods are permitted; everything must be inline.

i.    Using a loop built only on the % and / operators (no converting N to a String or array), compute, in the same loop:

•  the digit sum of N, and

•  the value of N with its digits reversed (e.g. for N = 4821, the reversed value is 1284).

ii.   Determine whether N is a palindrome by comparing N directly to the reversed value computed in step 1.

iii.  Inline in main() (not a separate method), determine whether the digit sum from step 1 is itself a prime number. Use a loop that tests divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum.

iv.  Using nested/chained conditional logic, classify N into exactly one of the following categories, checked strictly in this priority order:

•  "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM": if N is a palindrome AND its digit sum is prime

•  "PALINDROME": if N is a palindrome but its digit sum is not prime

•  "HARSHAD": if N is not a palindrome but N is exactly divisible by its own digit sum

•  "STANDARD": in every other case

v.   Display N, its digit sum, its reversed value, and its final classification in a single JOptionPane message dialog.

blocks.working:
Q6 a · classify a number by its digit pattern · 12 MARKS
  1. in one loop, built only on % and / (no converting N to a String or array), compute both the digit sum of N and N with its digits reversed;
  2. N is a palindrome if it equals its reversed value;
  3. inline, decide whether the digit sum is prime, testing divisibility only up to its square root;
  4. classify, strictly in this priority order: PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM (palindrome and sum prime), PALINDROME (palindrome, sum not prime), HARSHAD (not a palindrome, but N divides exactly by its digit sum), STANDARD otherwise;
  5. show N, its digit sum, its reversed value and its classification in a single dialog.
Must memorise · The digit loop, and the copy that saves it

Peeling digits off a number is three lines you should be able to write without thinking:

int digit = temp % 10;   takes the last digit
reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;   pushes it onto the right of the answer
temp = temp / 10;   drops the last digit

Loop while (temp > 0). Both answers fall out of one pass.

The line the marks hang on is int temp = n;. The loop destroys whatever it walks: temp ends at 0. Walk n itself and by step 2 there is nothing left to compare the reversed value against, and nothing left to divide in step 4. Copy it, consume the copy.

reversed * 10 + digit is worth a moment. Take 4821: the loop pulls 1, then 2, then 8, then 4. Start at 0, and each step shifts what you have one place left and drops the new digit into the units: 1, then 12, then 128, then 1284. The digits come off backwards, which is exactly why pushing them on in the order they arrive reverses the number.

MEMORY HOOK: % takes the last digit, / removes it. Every digit problem in this course is those two lines and a loop.

Teach · The square root test, without Math.sqrt

Part 3 says test divisibility only up to the square root of the digit sum. The clean way needs no square root at all:

boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {    if (digitSum % f == 0) { sumIsPrime = false; break; }}

f * f <= digitSum is "f is at most the square root of digitSum", squared on both sides. It stays in whole numbers, so there is no Math.sqrt, no double, and no floating-point comparison to get wrong at the boundary (Unit 3.6).

Why stopping at the square root is correct, not just faster. If digitSum = a * b, then a and b cannot both be above the square root, or their product would exceed digitSum. So every factor pairs with one at or below the square root. Find none there and there are none at all.

And the initialiser is the whole edge case. digitSum >= 2 is what makes 1 not prime and 0 not prime. The loop cannot help you: for digitSum = 1 it never runs, so whatever you started with survives. Start at true and the program declares 1 prime, and then N = 1 (a palindrome with digit sum 1) is misclassified. See the table below, last row.

Code · question six, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class PalindromeClassifier {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int n = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Step i: ONE loop, using only % and /, computing BOTH the digit sum and        // the reversed value. temp is consumed; n must survive for step ii.        int temp = n;        int digitSum = 0;        int reversed = 0;        while (temp > 0) {            int digit = temp % 10;            digitSum = digitSum + digit;            reversed = reversed * 10 + digit;            temp = temp / 10;        }        // Step ii: palindrome is a comparison against the ORIGINAL n.        boolean isPalindrome = (n == reversed);        // Step iii: is digitSum prime? Test factors only up to its square root.        boolean sumIsPrime = (digitSum >= 2);        for (int f = 2; f * f <= digitSum; f++) {            if (digitSum % f == 0) {                sumIsPrime = false;                break;            }        }        // Step iv: classify, in the paper's priority order.        String classification;        if (isPalindrome) {            if (sumIsPrime) {                classification = "PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM";            } else {                classification = "PALINDROME";            }        } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {            classification = "HARSHAD";        } else {            classification = "STANDARD";        }        // Step v: one dialog with all four facts.        String message = "N: " + n                       + "\nDigit sum: " + digitSum                       + "\nReversed: " + reversed                       + "\nClassification: " + classification;        System.out.println(message);    }}

Digit sum: 24
Reversed: 4884
Classification: PALINDROME

4884 is the paper's own example. It is a palindrome, and 24 = 2 × 12 is not prime, so it is PALINDROME and not PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM. That is the priority order doing its job.

Code · the same statements, run over every case · SO THE TABLE IS REAL

This is not the exam answer: the question forbids helper methods and demands a single N. It is the identical block of statements with a loop around it, so that every row below is real output rather than someone's arithmetic.

"PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM" : "PALINDROME";            } else if (n % digitSum == 0) {                classification = "HARSHAD";            } else {                classification = "STANDARD";            }            System.out.printf("%6d | %3d | %8d | %s%n", n, digitSum, reversed,                classification);        }    }}
Output     N | sum | reversed | classification
  4884 |  24 |     4884 | PALINDROME
     7 |   7 |        7 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
  4821 |  15 |     1284 | STANDARD
    21 |   3 |       12 | HARSHAD
   131 |   5 |      131 | PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM
     1 |   1 |        1 | PALINDROME

Six rows, and every branch of part 4 is exercised. 4884 and 4821 are the paper's own two examples and both come out as the paper says. 7 is its one-digit palindrome. 4821: the digit sum is 15 and 4821 = 15 × 321 + 6, so it is not a Harshad number either, and it falls to STANDARD. 1 is the row worth staring at: a palindrome whose digit sum is 1, and 1 is not prime, so PALINDROME. Get the initialiser wrong and this row alone would read PALINDROME-PRIME-SUM.

Trap · "Priority order" means else-if, not four ifs

Part 4 says checked strictly in this priority order and exactly one category. Both phrases point at the same structure: one chain, where reaching a test means every test above it already failed.

Write four independent ifs and a palindrome with a prime digit sum matches the first, then falls into the others too, and your single dialog reports whichever assignment landed last. The chain is what makes "exactly one" true, and it is also what makes HARSHAD's rule readable: HARSHAD never has to say "and is not a palindrome", because it is only ever reached when the palindrome test failed. The order does that work, which is precisely why the question fixes it (Unit 4.2).

Watch n % digitSum in the HARSHAD test. It is safe here only because N is a positive integer, so digitSum is at least 1 and never 0. Take that guarantee away and it throws ArithmeticException (Unit 3.6): a division by zero hiding in a remainder.

blocks.text: The parking garage, and three counts from one method

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed:
(13 marks)B. A university parking garage needs a program, using JOptionPane only for input/output, to process a batch of vehicles exiting on the same day and calculate the total fees owed. The program must use clear separation of concerns; each task below must be its own method. No collection classes (e.g. ArrayList) are allowed anywhere.

i.    Prompt for the number of exiting vehicles, V. Then, using a loop, fill two parallel arrays of length V:

•  the number of hours each vehicle was parked (an integer per vehicle). A value <= 0 is invalid; use a nested control statement to keep re-prompting until a valid value is entered.

•  the permit type for each vehicle (a String per vehicle, either "Staff" or "Visitor").

ii.   Create a method that takes in one vehicle's hours parked and permit type, and computes one vehicle's fee using nested if-else logic (the rules below must be nested together, not checked as separate independent conditions):

•  Staff: first 2 hours free; each additional hour costs 1.00; capped at a maximum of 10.00/day.

•  Visitor: no free period; first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00; each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50; capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

•  Any permit type that is not exactly "Staff" must be treated as "Visitor".

iii.  Create a method that takes in the array of hours parked, loops over the array and tallies vehicles into three categories: SHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs), STANDARD (3-6 hrs), EXTENDED (>6 hrs). Return these three counts without using any collection class.

iv.  In main(),

•  call the method from part (ii) for every vehicle across both parallel arrays to accumulate the batch's total revenue

•  call the method from part (iii) once

•  display one final JOptionPane showing the total revenue and the three category counts.

Q6 b · parking fees for a batch of vehicles · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt for the number of vehicles V, then fill two parallel arrays of length V: hours parked (int per vehicle; a value <= 0 is invalid, so use a nested control statement to re-prompt until valid) and permit type (String per vehicle, "Staff" or "Visitor");
  2. a method taking one vehicle's hours and permit, computing its fee with nested if-else: Staff, first 2 hours free, each additional hour 1.00, capped at 10.00/day; Visitor, no free period, first 3 hours a flat 6.00, each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50, capped at 25.00/day; and any permit that is not exactly "Staff" is treated as Visitor;
  3. a method taking the hours array, tallying SHORT-STAY (1-2), STANDARD (3-6) and EXTENDED (>6), returning the three counts without any collection class;
  4. main(): call (ii) for every vehicle across both arrays to accumulate revenue, call (iii) once, and display one dialog with the total and the three counts.
Must memorise · Three counts, one return, no collections

Part 3 asks for three numbers back. A Java method returns one value. And ArrayList is banned.

So return an int[] of length 3.

An array is not a collection class. That distinction is the question: "collection classes (e.g. ArrayList)" means java.util's List/Set/Map family. An array is a built-in Java type, not a class you import, which is why F.10 and Module 8 exist and why the ban costs you nothing.

Document the slots in a comment ([0] short, [1] standard, [2] extended) and use them in that order. The alternative the ban is steering you away from is three separate fields or three methods walking the same array three times.

MEMORY HOOK: one return value, several numbers, no collections: that is an array.

Teach · Parallel arrays, and the invariant that keeps them honest

Two arrays are parallel when index i in one and index i in the other describe the same thing. hoursParked[3] and permitType[3] are one car.

The whole idea rests on one invariant: they are the same length and they are always written together. The loop in part 1 fills both in the same iteration, which is what keeps them aligned. Fill them in two separate loops, or continue past one but not the other, and vehicle 3's hours are paired with vehicle 4's permit. Nothing throws. Every fee is simply wrong.

In Module 6's terms this is what a class is for: a Vehicle object holding hours and permit together cannot fall out of step, because there is no "step" to fall out of. The paper asks for parallel arrays, so write parallel arrays; but knowing what they are the poor relation of is what Q4 was testing.

Three counts, one return value, and no    // collection class: an int[] of length 3. An array is not a collection.    // [0] SHORT-STAY (1-2), [1] STANDARD (3-6), [2] EXTENDED (>6)    static int[] tally(int[] hoursParked) {        int[] counts = new int[3];        for (int i = 0; i < hoursParked.length; i++) {            if (hoursParked[i] <= 2) {                counts[0]++;            } else if (hoursParked[i] <= 6) {                counts[1]++;            } else {                counts[2]++;            }        }        return counts;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int vehicles = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Part i: two PARALLEL arrays. Index i is one vehicle in both.        int[] hoursParked = new int[vehicles];        String[] permitType = new String[vehicles];        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            int hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            while (hours <= 0) {                System.out.println("  vehicle " + i + ": " + hours                    + " is not a valid number of hours. Asking again.");                hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            }            hoursParked[i] = hours;            permitType[i] = in.nextLine();        }        // Part iv: accumulate revenue across both arrays, then tally once.        double totalRevenue = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            double fee = feeFor(hoursParked[i], permitType[i]);            totalRevenue += fee;            System.out.println("Vehicle " + i + ": " + hoursParked[i] + "h, "                + permitType[i] + " -> " + fee);        }        int[] counts = tally(hoursParked);        String message = "Total revenue: " + totalRevenue                       + "\nSHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs): " + counts[0]                       + "\nSTANDARD (3-6 hrs): " + counts[1]                       + "\nEXTENDED (>6 hrs): " + counts[2];        System.out.println(message);    }}

Vehicle 2: 15h, Staff -> 10.0
Vehicle 3: 1h, Visitor -> 6.0
Vehicle 4: 5h, Visitor -> 11.0

Every rule in the question fires exactly once in that table, which is how the test data was chosen: both free periods, both per-hour rates, both caps, and the not-Staff-means-Visitor rule. When you invent your own test data, invent it like this: one row per rule, so a single run proves the lot.

Two rows repay a second look. 1 hour as a Visitor costs 6.00: "first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00" is a flat fee, not a rate, so an hour and three hours cost the same, and a Visitor pays more than a Staff member who stayed fifteen. That is not a bug, it is the pricing the question specifies. And Guest at 12 hours is the only row testing the fallback rule; delete it from your test data and a program that crashes on unknown permits would look perfectly healthy.

Must memorise · A cap is a ceiling you apply after, not a rule you fold in

Compute the fee, then clamp it:

fee = 6.00 + (hours - 3) * 2.50;
if (fee > 25.00) { fee = 25.00; }

The temptation is to work out the hour at which the cap bites (for Visitors, 10.6 hours) and branch on that. It gives the same answers and it is a worse answer: you have hidden a magic number that no line of the question contains, and changing the rate to 3.00 silently breaks it, because the crossover moves and your constant does not.

This is the same shape as Q5 A's price floor, which is a cap from below. Both read as one line placed after the sum, and both then say plainly what the question said: capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

MEMORY HOOK: compute, then clamp. Never solve for where the clamp starts.

Q1 a · define method signature, overloading, and void method · 3 MARKS

Model answer. One mark each, and each is one sentence.

  1. Method signature. A method's name together with its parameter list (the number, types and order of its parameters). The return type is not part of the signature. It is what the compiler uses to tell one method from another.
  2. Method overloading. Declaring more than one method with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class, so the compiler chooses between them at compile time by matching the arguments at the call site against each signature.
  3. Void method. A method declared void, meaning it returns no value. It is called as a statement on its own, cannot be used in an expression, and may use a bare return; to exit early.

Where the marks are: the examiner asked for signature and overloading in the same breath deliberately, because the second is defined by the first. Say "signature = name + parameter list, return type excluded" and the overloading definition writes itself. Units 5.1, 5.2 and 5.6.

Q1 d · overload area for circle, rectangle and triangle · 7.5 MARKS
Must memorise · The obvious answer to this question does not compile

Circle needs one number. Rectangle needs two. Triangle needs two.

So rectangle is area(double, double), and triangle (base and height) is also area(double, double).

That is the same signature. It will not compile.

Overloading needs different parameter lists, and "base, height" is not different from "length, width": the parameter names are not part of the signature, only the types (Q1 A, which you just answered). Write both and javac says:

error: method area(double,double) is already defined in class

The resolution: give the triangle a three-number formula, so its signature is area(double, double, double) and distinct. Heron's formula takes the three sides:

s = (a + b + c) / 2     and     area = √ s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) 

MEMORY HOOK: overloads differ by types, not by names. If two of your methods take the same types in the same order, you have one method and a compiler error.

This is the single most valuable thing in Question One, and the examiner may not have noticed it. Say it explicitly in your answer: "base and height would collide with length and width, so the triangle is done by Heron's formula on three sides, giving a distinct signature." That sentence proves you understand overloading, which is what the question is for.

Three sides gives a distinct    // signature and a genuine formula: Heron's.    public static double area(double sideA, double sideB, double sideC) {        double s = (sideA + sideB + sideC) / 2;        return Math.sqrt(s * (s - sideA) * (s - sideB) * (s - sideC));    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        System.out.println("Circle, radius 7      : " + area(7.0));        System.out.println("Rectangle, 5 by 3     : " + area(5.0, 3.0));        System.out.println("Triangle, sides 3 4 5 : " + area(3.0, 4.0, 5.0));    }}

Q2 a · define dynamic array initialisation, length, and the out of bounds exception · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Dynamic array initialisation. Creating the array with new and a size decided while the program runs, rather than from a literal list written in the source: int[] a = new int[n]; where n is only known at run time. Every element starts at its default (0 for int, null for objects), and the values are filled in afterwards. Contrast static initialisation, int[] a = {2, 4, 6, 8};, where the size and the values are both fixed in the source.
  2. The length property. a.length gives the number of elements. It is a field, not a method, so there are no brackets: writing a.length() is a compile error. It is final: an array's length is fixed the moment it is created and can never change. A String's length IS a method, s.length(). The examiner knows that catches people; Unit 7.2.
  3. The out-of-bounds exception. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, thrown at run time when you use an index below 0 or at or above length. Valid indexes are 0 to length - 1, so a[a.length] always throws. It is unchecked, so the compiler will not warn you about it.

Where the marks are: "length is a field, not a method" and "indexes are 0 to length-1" are the two facts every other part of this question depends on. F.10 and Unit 8.1.

Q4 a · describe decision making, looping and branching · 3 MARKS

Model answer. These are the three families of control structure (Unit 4.1): the statements that decide which code runs and how often, rather than doing the work themselves.

  1. Decision-making. Choosing between paths by testing a condition, so that some code runs and some does not: if, if-else, the if-else ladder, and switch.
  2. Looping (iteration). Repeating a block while a condition holds: for, while and do-while. The do-while is the one that always runs at least once, because it tests at the bottom.
  3. Branching (jumping). Transferring control out of the normal flow: break leaves a loop or a switch case, continue skips to the next iteration, and return leaves the method entirely.

Q5 a · describe inheritance, polymorphism and method overriding · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Inheritance. One class acquiring the fields and methods of another with extends, so the subclass has everything the superclass has without repeating it, and may add or replace behaviour. It models an is-a relationship: a Bicycle is a Vehicle.
  2. Polymorphism. One reference, many behaviours: a variable of the superclass type may hold an object of any subclass, and a call through it runs the object's own version, decided at run time. "Many forms".
  3. Method overriding. A subclass supplying its own version of a method the superclass already has, with the same signature, which replaces the inherited one for objects of that subclass.

Where the marks are: these three are one idea in three parts, and saying so earns the mark. Inheritance makes the family; overriding makes the members differ; polymorphism is what you get when you then hold any of them in one variable and call the method. Distinguish overriding (same signature, subclass, run time) from overloading (different parameters, same class, compile time), which is Q1 of this same paper. Units 6.6 and 6.7.

Trap · The paper contradicts itself, and you must answer anyway

Read the second example again. It says "1223 - true" and then, in the same line, "Only one pair - return false". Both cannot be right.

The specification says "at least two pairs". 1223 has one pair, the 22. One is not at least two.

The correct return is false. The leading "true" is a slip of the pen.

The examiner's own explanation ("Only one pair") agrees with the specification, so the specification and the reasoning outvote the stray word. This book shows you the paper exactly as printed and tells you what is true, and it never quietly corrects a source (compare the six errors in Module 3, which come from this course's own slides).

What to do in the hall. Do not agonise, and do not answer the typo. Implement the specification, and write one line saying why: "1223 has only one adjacent pair, so by the stated rule of at least two pairs the method returns false; the 'true' in the example appears to be a typographical error." That sentence costs ten seconds and it protects you whichever way the marking scheme reads, because it proves the answer was a decision and not a mistake.

Code · q6 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class AdjacentPairs {    // i/ii. true when n has AT LEAST TWO pairs of equal adjacent digits.    public static boolean hasEqualAdjacentPairs(int n) {        int pairs = 0;        int previous = n % 10;        n = n / 10;        while (n > 0) {            int current = n % 10;            if (current == previous) {                pairs++;            }            previous = current;            n = n / 10;        }        return pairs >= 2;    }    // iii b. main testing more than the two cases the question asks for    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] tests = {112233, 1223, 1122, 111, 123, 7, 122333};        for (int t : tests) {            System.out.println(t + " -> " + hasEqualAdjacentPairs(t));        }    }}

1223 -> false
1122 -> true
111 -> true
123 -> false
7 -> false
122333 -> true

The paper asks for at least two test cases; there are seven, and each earns its place. 112233 and 1223 are the paper's own. 1122 is the boundary: exactly two pairs, so exactly true. 111 asks what a triple counts as. 123 has no pairs and 7 has no adjacent digits at all, so the loop never runs and pairs stays 0.

Must memorise · Compare adjacent digits by remembering the last one

Take the last digit before the loop and call it previous. Then each turn: take the new current, compare it with previous, and make current the new previous.

That is the whole technique, and it is the same % 10 and / 10 pair as Q6 A on the 2025/26 paper. The only new idea is carrying one value forward so that each digit can see its neighbour. You never need the digits in an array; you need exactly one of them remembered.

111 gives two pairs, not one. The digits are compared in overlapping pairs: positions 1-2 and 2-3. The middle 1 belongs to both. If you think a triple should count once, that is a different specification, and this one does not say so: it says pairs of equal adjacent digits, and 111 contains two of them.

MEMORY HOOK: to compare neighbours, remember one. Peel a digit, compare, then let it become the memory for the next.

JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Total: " + t) Shows a message. Returns nothing. The null is the parent window: there isn't one.
System.exit(0) Ends the program. 0 means "ended normally". See F.11: it is insurance, not a rescue.

MEMORY HOOK: showInput asks, showMessage tells. Input comes back as text, so it always needs converting.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: Text to number, because a dialog only ever gives you text
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does, and what to watch
Integer.parseInt(s) String to int. Throws NumberFormatException if s is not a whole number.
Double.parseDouble(s) String to double. Same exception on nonsense.

The full shape, which you will write a dozen times on one paper:

int age = Integer.parseInt(JOptionPane.showInputDialog(null, "Age:"));

MEMORY HOOK: the dialog hands you a String even when you asked for a number. Every input is two steps: ask, then convert.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The file I/O the paper allows
blocks.html:
The 2025/26 Question Three names five classes and permits nothing else: FileWriter, FileReader, BufferedReader, BufferedWriter, IOException.

CallWhat it does, and what to watch
new FileWriter("f.txt") Opens for writing. Creates the file if absent, and truncates it if present.
new FileWriter("f.txt", true) The same, but appends. This second argument is the only way to append, and it belongs here, on the writer that touches the disk.
new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter("f.txt")) Wraps a writer and writes in blocks. Gives you newLine().
new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("f.txt", true)) Wraps a writer and gives you printf() and println() on a file. Note new PrintWriter("f.txt") on its own truncates and cannot append.
new BufferedReader(new FileReader("f.txt")) Opens for reading, in blocks. Gives you readLine().
readLine() The next line, or null at the end of the file. That null is the loop's stopping condition.
try (BufferedReader in = ...) { } try-with-resources. Closes it whether the block ends normally or by throwing. Nothing to forget.
catch (IOException e) Checked: catch it or declare throws, or it will not compile.

MEMORY HOOK: Reader in, Writer out; Buffered wraps; Print formats. The one that touches the disk carries the append flag.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: printf, and the four formats that cover every paper
blocks.html:
FormatMeans
%da whole number
%fa decimal. %.2f means two decimal places.
%sa string. %-8s means left-aligned in 8 columns.
%nend the line. Use this, not \n.

printf rounds the digits you wrote, half up, so your paper arithmetic is trustworthy: %.2f of 1.005 really is 1.01. See MS.4, where that was measured against 99,999 values.

MEMORY HOOK: width before the point, precision after. %-8.2f is "left-aligned, eight wide, two decimals".

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: System: printing, and two things that are not printing
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does
System.out.println(x)Prints x, then ends the line.
System.out.print(x)Prints x and stays on the line.
System.out.printf(fmt, ...)Formatted printing. Ends no line unless you write %n.
System.exit(0)Stops the JVM at once. 0 means normal.
System.arraycopy(src, a, dst, b, n)Copies n elements from src at a into dst at b. Note the lower-case c: arrayCopy does not exist.
System.console()The terminal, or null when there isn't one. Returns a Console.
System.inThe keyboard, as a stream. Only ever seen inside new Scanner(System.in).

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Math: no import needed, and every method is static
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does
Math.PI3.141592653589793. A constant, so no brackets.
Math.abs(x)The size of x, sign removed.
Math.max(a, b)The larger.
Math.min(a, b)The smaller.
Math.pow(a, b)a to the power b, always a double. See Unit 3.6: it is exact for the sizes this course uses.
Math.sqrt(x)The square root, as a double. For a primality test prefer d * d <= n, which stays in integers.
Math.round(x)Nearest whole number, halves going up. Returns long for a double.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: String: the text type, and it never changes
blocks.html:
Every method here returns a new String. None of them alters the one you called it on, because a String cannot be altered (Unit 7.1). If you do not keep the answer, nothing happened.

CallWhat it does
length()How many characters. A method on a String, unlike an array's length.
charAt(i)The character at index i, counting from 0.
substring(from)From from to the end.
substring(from, to)From from up to but not including to.
indexOf(s)Where s starts, or -1 if it is absent.
contains(s)true if s is in there.
startsWith(s)true if it begins with s.
endsWith(s)true if it ends with s.
toUpperCase()A new String, in capitals.
isEmpty()true only if there are no characters. A space is a character.
concat(s)A new String with s joined on. The + operator does the same.
replace(a, b)A new String with every a swapped for b.
equals(s)Compares the characters. This is the one you want (Unit 7.3).
equalsIgnoreCase(s)The same, treating "JAVA" and "java" as equal.
compareTo(s)Negative, zero or positive, by dictionary order.
new String("hi")Forces a brand new object. It exists to demonstrate why == is wrong for text, and for no other reason.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: StringBuilder: the text type that does change
blocks.html:
The mirror image of String: every method here alters the builder itself and you do not keep a return value (Unit 7.4).

CallWhat it does
new StringBuilder("Java")A builder holding "Java".
append(x)Adds x to the end.
insert(i, s)Pushes s in so it starts at i, sliding the rest right. Nothing is lost.
delete(a, b)Removes from a up to but not including b.
replace(a, b, s)Removes a to b, then puts s there. Can change the length.
reverse()Turns it back to front.
toString()The finished text, as a String.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does
ArraysThe toolkit class. import java.util.Arrays;. Every method on it is static.
lengthThe size of an array. A field: a.length, never a.length(). The last index is always length - 1.
Arrays.toString(a)The array as readable text. Printing a directly gives you a hash code.
Arrays.sort(a)Sorts a in place. Returns nothing.
Arrays.copyOf(a, n)A new array of length n, padded or trimmed.
Arrays.equals(a, b)Compares the contents. a == b compares the references.
Arrays.asList(x, y)The arguments as a list, for the one place this course needs one: Files.write.

The exam bans collection classes and asks for parallel arrays instead: two arrays of the same length where index i means the same subject in both.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Reading the keyboard: Scanner, and the two alternatives
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does
ScannerThe class. import java.util.Scanner;.
new Scanner(System.in)A scanner on the keyboard.
nextLine()The whole next line, as a String.
nextInt()The next whole number. Leaves the newline behind, which is why a following nextLine() returns empty (Unit 3.10).
hasNextLine()true while a line is waiting. Ask before you take, instead of comparing against a sentinel.
close()Releases it. Every reader and writer has one.
new InputStreamReader(System.in)Turns the raw keyboard stream into something a reader can read.
new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in))The older way to read the keyboard. Its readLine() returns a String.
ConsoleThe class System.console() hands back. It is null in every IDE, which is the whole lesson of Unit 3.10.
readPassword()On a Console: reads without echoing. Returns a char[], not a String.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Files: the classic way, which the paper demands
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does
new FileWriter(name)Opens for writing. Creates, or truncates.
new FileWriter(name, true)Opens for appending.
new FileReader(name)Opens for reading.
new BufferedWriter(w)Wraps a writer, writing in blocks.
new BufferedReader(r)Wraps a reader, reading in blocks.
new PrintWriter(w)Wraps a writer and adds printf and println.
new File(name)A file name, not a file. Creating one opens nothing.
write(s)Writes text. On a FileWriter or BufferedWriter.
newLine()Ends the line, on a BufferedWriter.
read()One character, as an int, or -1 at the end of the file.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Files: the modern one-liners, and the 24/25 question that names them
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does
Paths.get("f.txt")A Path: a file name in the form the Files methods want.
Files.write(path, lines)Writes every line and closes the file, in one call.
Files.readAllLines(path)The whole file, as a list of lines.
Files.readAllBytes(path)The whole file, as raw bytes.

The 2024/25 Question Three A asks you to define Files.write(). Learn these four, and then use the classic classes in Section B, because the 2025/26 paper bans everything but them.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: Exceptions, and the wrappers that throw them
blocks.html:
NameWhat it is
ExceptionThe parent of nearly all of them. catch (Exception e) catches everything below it, which is why it must come last, and why catching it instead of the specific one is a way of not saying what you expected to go wrong.
IOExceptionChecked. Anything went wrong with a file. Catch it or declare it.
FileNotFoundExceptionChecked. A subclass of IOException, so catch it first or it is unreachable.
NumberFormatExceptionUnchecked. parseInt met something that is not a number.
ArithmeticExceptionUnchecked. Integer division by zero. Decimal division by zero gives Infinity instead.
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptionUnchecked. An index below 0 or at length or above.
NullPointerExceptionUnchecked. A method was called on null.
new IllegalArgumentException("why")Unchecked. Throw it yourself when an argument makes no sense.
new ArithmeticException("why")Throwing one yourself, to show throw against throws.
getMessage()The text carried by the exception.
getClass()The object's class, at run time.
getSimpleName()On a class: its name without the package, so IOException rather than java.io.IOException.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: The wrapper classes and their constants
blocks.html:
CallWhat it does
Integer.parseInt(s)String to int.
Double.parseDouble(s)String to double.
Integer.MAX_VALUE2147483647. Use the constant, not the digits: your course's own table mistyped them.
Integer.MIN_VALUE-2147483648.
Long.MAX_VALUE9223372036854775807.
Long.MIN_VALUE-9223372036854775808.
Integer.toBinaryString(n)n written in binary, as text.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
KeywordWhat it means
byteA whole number, 8 bits, -128 to 127.
shortA whole number, 16 bits, -32768 to 32767.
intA whole number, 32 bits. The default for any whole number you type.
longA whole number, 64 bits. A big literal needs an L: 9000000000L.
floatA decimal, 32 bits. A literal needs an f: 3.14f.
doubleA decimal, 64 bits. The default for any decimal you type.
charOne character, in single quotes: 'J'.
booleantrue or false, and nothing else. Not 0 and 1.
trueOne of the two boolean values.
falseThe other.
null"Refers to no object." Not zero, and not an empty string.
voidAs a return type: this method gives nothing back.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
KeywordWhat it means
ifRun the block only when the condition is true.
elseOtherwise. It arrives already knowing what failed.
switchChoose a branch by matching a value against cases.
caseOne value a switch matches.
defaultThe switch branch for everything unmatched.
forA counting loop: init, test and update on one line.
whileA loop that tests before the body, so it can run zero times.
doWith while: a loop that tests after, so it always runs once.
breakLeaves the loop at once. In a switch, ends that case.
continueSkips the rest of this turn and goes to the next. It does not leave the loop.
returnLeaves the method, carrying a value unless the method is void.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
KeywordWhat it means
classDeclares a class: the blueprint an object is made from.
newMakes an object and runs its constructor.
thisThe object the method was called on. Used to tell a field from a parameter of the same name.
staticBelongs to the class, not to any object. Called as ClassName.method().
finalCannot be changed after it is set. The way to write a constant.
publicVisible everywhere.
privateVisible only inside this class. Not even a subclass can name it.
protectedVisible inside this class and its subclasses.
extendsThis class inherits from that one.
superThe superclass part of this object: super(...) calls its constructor, super.m() its method.
abstractIncomplete on purpose: it cannot be instantiated, and a subclass must finish it.
interfaceA contract of method signatures with no bodies.
implementsThis class promises to supply an interface's methods.
importNames a class from another package so you can use its short name.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
KeywordWhat it means
tryGuard this block. With brackets, it also closes what it opened.
catchHandle an exception of the named type. Catch subclasses first.
finallyRuns whatever happens, exception or not.
throwRaises an exception now: throw new IllegalArgumentException("...").
throwsDeclares that this method may raise one, and refuses to handle it.

MEMORY HOOK: throw does, throws warns. The s is a signature, not an action.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.tag: The keywords this course does not use are still reserved
blocks.html:
Java has fifty reserved words. This book uses the forty-two above, because they are the ones your course teaches and your papers examine. The rest are real and you may not use them as names either:

assert, const, enum, goto, instanceof, native, package, strictfp, synchronized, transient, volatile.

Two of those are curiosities worth ten seconds: const and goto are reserved and do nothing at all. They exist only so that the compiler can give you a proper error instead of a confusing one if you arrive from a language that has them. Java's constant is final.

They are listed here rather than tabled above for one reason: this book documents what it uses. An entry claiming to teach you synchronized would be a promise no page of this manual keeps.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
TermDefinition
Source codeThe Java you type, in a .java file. Text, readable by people.
Compiler (javac)Translates source into bytecode, and refuses if the source is not legal Java.
BytecodeThe .class file. Not machine code, and not tied to any one processor.
JVMThe Java Virtual Machine: the program that runs bytecode. The reason Java runs anywhere.
JDKThe kit: compiler, JVM, and libraries. You need it to write Java, not merely to run it.
Compile-time errorThe code is not legal Java. Nothing runs. The compiler tells you the line.
Run-time errorLegal code that hits something impossible while running. Java throws an exception.
Logic errorIt compiles, it runs, it finishes, and the answer is wrong. Nothing warns you. Only a dry run finds it.
Dry runExecuting a program by hand, one row per step, writing down every variable as it changes. Your lecturer's own term, and an exam skill.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
TermDefinition
VariableA named box holding one value of a declared type.
Primitive typeOne of the eight built-in types. The variable holds the value itself.
Reference typeEverything else. The variable holds a reference to an object stored elsewhere.
LiteralA value written directly in the code: 42, 3.14, "hi". Its type is fixed when you type it, before anything is assigned.
ConstantA final variable: set once, never changed.
CastingTelling the compiler to convert a type, taking responsibility for the loss: (int) 3.9 is 3.
WideningA smaller type flowing into a bigger one automatically, losing nothing: an int into a double.
NarrowingThe reverse, which loses data, so Java never does it silently.
Integer division/ between two whole numbers, which chops the remainder away. 7 / 2 is 3. It does not round.
ArrayA fixed-length run of values of one type, reached by index from 0.
IndexAn element's position. The last is always length - 1.
Parallel arraysTwo or more arrays of equal length where the same index means the same subject. This course's substitute for a collection.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
TermDefinition
MethodA named, reusable block that may take values in and may give one back.
Formal parameterThe variable named in the method's declaration. A name waiting for a value.
Actual argumentThe value written at the call, which is copied into the parameter.
Method signatureThe name plus the parameter list. The return type is not part of it.
Return typeThe type of what comes back, or void for nothing.
OverloadingSeveral methods, same name, different parameter lists. Resolved at compile time. Compile-time polymorphism.
OverridingA subclass replacing an inherited method with the same signature. Resolved at run time.
Pass by valueJava's only mechanism. The value is copied. For a reference type, the reference is copied, so the method can change the object but cannot make your variable point elsewhere.
RecursionA method that calls itself, with a base case that stops it.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
TermDefinition
ClassThe blueprint: what an object of this kind knows and can do.
ObjectOne thing made from that blueprint, with its own copy of the state.
Attribute (field)A variable belonging to an object: what it knows.
ConstructorRuns once, at new, to put a new object into a valid state. Named exactly like the class, and declares no return type at all.
Instance methodBelongs to an object. Called on one: account.deposit(500).
Static methodBelongs to the class. Called on it: Math.abs(-3).
EncapsulationKeeping state private and exposing it through methods, so an object controls its own data.
InheritanceA subclass acquiring the superclass's members with extends. An is-a relationship.
PolymorphismOne name, several behaviours. Compile-time is overloading; run-time is overriding.
Dynamic method dispatchThe run-time half: the object decides which override runs, not the reference's declared type.
AbstractionExposing what a thing does and hiding how. In Java: abstract classes and interfaces.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
TermDefinition
ExceptionAn object describing something that went wrong, thrown at the point of failure.
Checked exceptionThe compiler insists you catch it or declare it. IOException. A fact about the world, not a bug.
Unchecked exceptionNot policed. NullPointerException. Usually a bug, so the fix is to correct the code, not to catch it.
try-with-resourcestry (Reader r = ...): closes what it opened, on every path, including the throwing one.
StreamA one-way flow of data. A reader reads one; a writer writes one.
BufferingCollecting data and moving it in blocks rather than one character at a time.
SentinelA value that means "stop", chosen so it cannot be real data: readLine() gives null, read() gives -1.

blocks.label: Must memorise
blocks.tag: The five definitions both papers keep asking for
blocks.html:
Across 2024/25 and 2025/26, these came up again and again. If you learn five definitions, learn these, in these words:

1. Method signature: the method's name plus its parameter list. The return type is not part of it.
2. Overloading against overriding: same name different parameters, settled at compile time; against same signature in a subclass, settled at run time.
3. Checked against unchecked: the compiler forces you to handle a checked one, or it will not compile.
4. Encapsulation: private state, public methods, so the object owns its own data.
5. Dry run: hand-execute the code, one row per step.

MEMORY HOOK: every one of these is a distinction, not a fact. The mark is in the contrast, so answer in two halves and say which is which.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
You have the machine underneath, the ten modules, both real papers solved, two mocks sat and marked, and this reference. Nothing in this book was taken on trust: every listing was compiled and run, every printed output came off a real JVM, and every claim about what the compiler says was made by asking it.

Where your course materials and the compiler disagreed, this book says so and shows you the run. That is not disrespect. It is the only habit that matters in programming: the machine is the authority, and it will tell you, and you can ask it any time you like.

Go and ask it. Then go and pass.
